Optics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 97k Articles: 1k
Optics studies light, its propagation, and instruments for forming images and measuring optical spectra.
The central question is how light carries information from a source to an observer. A useful description must explain both where the light goes and how its distribution changes. In geometrical optics, light rays locate paths and images; in physical optics, an electromagnetic wave has a wave amplitude and a wave phase, so overlapping contributions can produce wave interference and diffraction. These descriptions address different levels of detail within the same subject. [ref].
An image is especially interesting because a single object point emits light in many directions. An optical lens redirects part of that spreading bundle toward a corresponding image point; repeating this construction over the object preserves spatial information. Simply gathering more light is insufficient: light rays from distinct object points must arrive at distinct locations. This is why an optical camera needs both an optical lens and a correctly positioned receiving surface. The thin lens example below makes that correspondence quantitative. [ref].

Structural coloration

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Colour produced through wavelength-dependent interaction with spatial structure, such as thin-film interference or diffraction, rather than pigment absorption alone.

Nacre

Words: 26
Structural coloration OurBigBook.com
A layered biomineral in shells and pearls. Repeating mineral–organic layers can produce interference colour, while oriented surface grooves can also diffract light.[ref]

Illuminant

Words: 24
Optics OurBigBook.com
A specified spectral distribution of illumination. A real scene can contain several sources and reflected illumination, so one global illuminant spectrum is a simplification.

Subsurface scattering

Words: 27
Optics OurBigBook.com
Transport in which light enters a material, scatters within it and exits, potentially at another surface location. A purely local surface-reflection model does not describe all such transport.

Luminance (Lv​)

Words: 49
Optics OurBigBook.com
A photometric measure of directional light output weighted by a specified luminous-efficiency function, conventionally measured in candela per square metre. It is distinct from illuminance, which concerns light incident per unit area, and from perceived brightness. Chromatic-discrimination experiments must control luminance cues when those cues could reveal the answer.

Linear optics

Words: 53
Optics OurBigBook.com
In linear optics, the response is linear in the optical field and propagation or passive mixing maps mode annihilation operators to linear combinations of mode annihilation operators. Wave plates and beam splitters can rotate or mix photonic modes, but do not by themselves supply a deterministic interaction between independent photon-number qubits. Conditional measurements and auxiliary photons change that resource model.

Saturable absorption

Words: 52 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Absorption that decreases with increasing illumination intensity as the absorber's population distribution changes. It can provide an intensity-dependent loss for passive Q-switching.

Saturable absorber

Words: 30
Saturable absorption OurBigBook.com
An element whose transmission increases as its absorption saturates. In a passive Q-switched laser it initially blocks oscillation, then becomes more transparent when the growing intracavity field bleaches the loss.

Metamerism (color)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Distinct spectra can give the same colour response for a specified observer and illumination. In a simplified three-cone cell model, equal values of ∫L(λ)R(λ)Si​(λ)dλ for i=1,2,3 need not imply identical spectral reflectance functions R. Altering illumination or observer can break the match.

Metamer

Words: 33
Metamerism (color) OurBigBook.com
A stimulus belonging to a pair of physically different optical spectra that match for a specified observer and viewing condition. Such a match exhibits metamerism. Changing the observer, adaptation or illumination can break the match.

Optical microscopy

Words: 67 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Investigation using a light-based optical microscope. Resolution, specimen preparation and interpretation constrain what can be established from an image.

Three-dimensional reconstruction from serial sections (V=∫A(z)dz)

Words: 49
Optical microscopy OurBigBook.com
Aligned two-dimensional sections constrain the three-dimensional structure of a specimen. For parallel sections of known spacing Δz, the Riemann sum ∑i​Ai​Δz approximates volume. Distortion, missing sections and alignment errors constrain the reconstruction; the volume estimate alone does not determine the identity or developmental fate of each visible structure.

Motion blur

Words: 77
Optics OurBigBook.com
Motion blur arises when a detector averages changing image positions during a finite exposure rather than recording an instantaneous position. For a stationary harmonic optical trap with position variance kB​T/k and relaxation time τ, rectangular exposure of duration W reduces that variance by the factor 2[α−1+e−α]/α2, where α=W/τ. Integrating the exponential position covariance over both exposure times proves this formula. Ignoring the reduction makes a naive equipartition stiffness estimate too large.[ref]

Photonic structure

Words: 37
Optics OurBigBook.com
A designed spatial arrangement of dielectric or other electromagnetic material controls optical propagation, confinement or emission. Examples include waveguides, distributed Bragg reflectors, photonic crystals and defect cavities. Spatial interference and mode boundary conditions act on electromagnetic states; they are distinct from the electronic band structure of the material itself.

Photonic crystal

Words: 135 Articles: 4
Optics OurBigBook.com
A structure with spatially periodic dielectric response, giving optical bands and, under suitable conditions, forbidden frequency intervals.

Photonic band structure

Words: 86 Articles: 2
Photonic crystal OurBigBook.com
The frequencies ωn​(k) of electromagnetic Bloch modes form allowed bands in a periodic dielectric. Their gaps and curvature determine forbidden propagation, confinement and group velocity.

Photonic band gap

Words: 61 Articles: 1
Photonic band structure OurBigBook.com
A frequency interval without bulk propagating electromagnetic modes in the specified directions and polarizations. A complete gap excludes all directions and polarizations; a one-dimensional stop band need not do so.
Photonic-crystal defect localization
Words: 32
Photonic band gap OurBigBook.com
A local departure from periodicity can support a discrete mode inside a bulk photonic band gap. An isolated defect makes a cavity; a line of defects may guide light. Finite surrounding crystals allow leakage.

Colloidal photonic crystal

Words: 32
Photonic crystal OurBigBook.com
An ordered array of colloidal building blocks whose optical-scale periodicity gives Bragg reflection and photonic stop bands. Particle size and refractive-index contrast control the response; defects and stacking disorder can broaden it.

Distributed Bragg reflector

Words: 80 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
A multilayer reflector using constructive interference of reflections from alternating refractive-index layers.

Quarter-wave Bragg stack (nH​dH​=nL​dL​=λ0​/4)

Words: 69
Distributed Bragg reflector OurBigBook.com
At normal incidence, alternating layers with indices nH​,nL​ and optical thicknesses nH​dH​=nL​dL​=λ0​/4 give reinforcing reflected waves near design wavelength λ0​. Their periodic transfer matrix has a stop band when its Bloch phase is complex. A finite stack has nonzero transmission and its exterior impedances matter. Introducing a suitably phased central defect can support a transmission resonance within the stop band; a one-dimensional stop band is not a complete three-dimensional photonic gap.

Color vision

Words: 1k Articles: 32
Optics OurBigBook.com
Color vision distinguishes distributions of visible light across wavelengths through the different spectral sensitivities of visual receptors. A perceived colour need not correspond to one wavelength: different optical spectra can produce the same receptor responses. Consequently the broad spectral filtering of thin-film interference need not produce pure monochromatic colours.

Color naming

Words: 23
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Assigning linguistic labels to color stimuli or appearances. Shared naming, discrimination and matching must be measured separately; one observation does not define the others.

Colorimetry

Words: 209 Articles: 5
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Measurement and specification of color-related stimulus relations, especially matches and coordinates for stated observers and conditions. Device values require spectral and radiometric calibration before they can be interpreted as cone stimulation.

Display calibration

Words: 32
Colorimetry OurBigBook.com
Measurement and adjustment of a display's spectral, intensity and temporal output relative to control settings. The emitted primary spectra and their nonlinear control functions matter; RGB numbers alone do not specify retinal stimulation.

Silent substitution

Words: 44
Colorimetry OurBigBook.com
A stimulus manipulation designed to vary one receptor class while holding others approximately fixed. With a calibrated primary-to-receptor matrix B, solve for primary changes producing a specified catch change, respecting baseline and gamut constraints. Observer variation, calibration error and unintended receptor inputs can limit isolation.

Gamut

Words: 48
Colorimetry OurBigBook.com
The set of stimuli or coordinates realizable by a specified device or system. If primary intensities p are bounded and nonnegative and cone catches satisfy Q=Bp, invertibility of B does not ensure feasibility: a requested B−1Q can lie outside the permitted primary ranges.

Color chromaticity

Words: 28
Colorimetry OurBigBook.com
Color information considered apart from an overall intensity coordinate under a stated colorimetric convention. It is distinct from accelerator chromaticity and should not be confused with a complete appearance description.

Color space

Words: 26
Colorimetry OurBigBook.com
A coordinate representation of color stimuli or responses under stated conventions. Euclidean separation in a chosen space need not equal perceptual discriminability for every observer and task.

Color constancy

Words: 78 Articles: 1
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Relative stability of perceived surface color across changes in illumination or viewing conditions. The measured degree depends on task, adaptation and available cues. Perfect physical recovery is impossible in unrestricted scenes because illumination and reflectance can be nonunique.

Surface-illuminant ambiguity

Words: 42
Color constancy OurBigBook.com
In a diffuse spectral model N(λ)=E(λ)R(λ), choose any positive g for which R/g remains an admissible reflectance. Then E′=Eg and R′=R/g preserve N exactly. Thus outgoing spectral information alone does not uniquely identify reflectance and illumination; three-channel receptor sampling introduces further ambiguity.

Color appearance

Words: 216 Articles: 6
Color vision OurBigBook.com
The experienced color of a stimulus under specified viewing, adaptation and contextual conditions. Appearance judgments, discrimination thresholds and naming are related but different observations.

Achromatic point

Words: 44
Color appearance OurBigBook.com
A stimulus setting judged to have no chromatic tint under stated conditions. An observer adjusting a patch to cancel a perceived tint moves the physical setting in a compensating direction; the adjustment must not be confused with the direction of the original appearance shift.

Lightness

Words: 25
Color appearance OurBigBook.com
Perceived surface achromatic reflectance, often judged relative to a white reference. The same outgoing luminance can support different lightness interpretations under different illumination or scene context.

Brightness

Words: 21
Color appearance OurBigBook.com
Perceived amount or intensity of light from a stimulus. It is distinct from physical luminance and from lightness as a judgment related to surface reflectance.

Hue

Words: 103 Articles: 2
Color appearance OurBigBook.com
The color attribute distinguishing appearances such as red, yellow, green or blue and their combinations. A hue need not identify a single wavelength, and cone-class labels do not directly specify it.
Unique hue
Words: 73 Articles: 1
Hue OurBigBook.com
A hue judged to contain no perceptual mixture of a specified opponent pair, such as a yellow judged neither reddish nor greenish. Its measured setting depends on observer and conditions and should not simply be identified with one retinal cardinal axis.
Unique yellow
Words: 33
Unique hue OurBigBook.com
A yellow judged neither reddish nor greenish. A wavelength or matching setting can operationalize the judgment under controlled conditions; shifts in that setting do not by themselves identify the neural locus of a change.

Cone contrast (cj​=(Qj​−Qj0​)/Qj0​)

Words: 38
Color vision OurBigBook.com
A receptor catch change expressed relative to a positive adapted-background catch. The same absolute increment can represent different contrasts on different backgrounds. These coordinates are useful for isolating signals without asserting that all neurons explicitly divide in this way.

Opponent color processing (gL​QL​−gM​QM​)

Words: 189 Articles: 3
Color vision OurBigBook.com
A class of post-receptoral computations comparing signals from different cone populations, for example a gain-weighted L–M difference and an S versus L+M comparison. Such comparisons distinguish spectral differences from shared changes in illumination intensity. Receptor counts, signal gains and later appearance judgments need not vary proportionally.

Cardinal directions of color space

Words: 44
Opponent color processing OurBigBook.com
Stimulus directions distinguished by selective adaptation or physiological response nulls under specified conditions, commonly associated with an achromatic-like combination and two cone-opponent combinations. Their usefulness near a particular background does not make them identical to unique-hue directions or sufficient for every suprathreshold appearance judgment.

Chromatic null plane (wTc=0)

Words: 60
Opponent color processing OurBigBook.com
If a nonzero weight vector combines cone contrasts as r=wTc, its zero-response contrasts satisfy one linear constraint and form a two-dimensional plane through the adapted origin in three-dimensional contrast space. Any two independent vectors in that plane constrain the direction of the normal w, up to scale. Nonlinearities and response noise limit empirical identification.

Invertible three-channel opponent transform

Words: 39
Opponent color processing OurBigBook.com
The illustrative transform y0​=cL​+cM​, y1​=cL​−cM​, y2​=cS​−(cL​+cM​)/2 has determinant −2. Solving gives cL​=(y0​+y1​)/2, cM​=(y0​−y1​)/2 and cS​=y2​+y0​/2. Thus it reorganizes three cone coordinates without adding independent spectral information. Biological response weights and nonlinearities are further empirical questions.

Color discrimination

Words: 30
Color vision OurBigBook.com
The ability to distinguish stimuli using their chromatic differences under stated conditions. Controlled tests suppress luminance and other unintended cues and estimate a psychometric function. Color matching, color naming and discrimination are different observations.

Tetrachromacy

Words: 41
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Color vision using four functionally independent spectral channels. Four pigment variants or four potential cone cell types do not alone demonstrate four-dimensional behavioral discrimination. Tests must establish information use beyond the matches available to a specified trichromat.[ref]

Color matching

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Color vision OurBigBook.com
An observer adjusts lights until they appear to match a comparison under specified viewing and adaptation conditions. The settings and range of accepted matches constrain the available spectral signals. Matching differs from detecting a difference and from assigning a color name.

Rayleigh color match

Words: 42
Color matching OurBigBook.com
A match between a mixture of two long/middle-wave lights and a comparison light, with mixture ratio and brightness separately adjustable. The settings and acceptance range help characterize red–green color-vision variation. A satisfactory brightness match alone is not evidence for normal chromatic discrimination.

Colour vision model

Words: 86 Articles: 2
Color vision OurBigBook.com
A model relating a stimulus to the inputs and discrimination capacity of a visual system. Receiver spectral sensitivity, illumination and background matter; human colour distances are not automatically perceptual distances for another animal.

Receptor noise

Words: 21
Colour vision model OurBigBook.com
Variability in a sensory receptor signal that limits discrimination. A difference in average receptor quantum catch does not alone establish a perceptually discriminable difference.

Receptor quantum catch (Qi​)

Words: 33
Colour vision model OurBigBook.com
Expected photon absorption by a receptor class. A simple relative model is Qi​=∫L(λ)R(λ)Si​(λ)dλ, with illumination L, object reflectance R and effective spectral sensitivity Si​. Absolute catch also requires geometric and temporal factors.

Dichromacy

Words: 9
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Colour vision based on two classes of photoreceptor input.

Trichromacy

Words: 60 Articles: 1
Color vision OurBigBook.com
Colour vision based on three classes of photoreceptor input. Functional discrimination must be tested rather than inferred solely from gene count.

Anomalous trichromacy

Words: 39
Trichromacy OurBigBook.com
Color vision with three independent receptor classes whose spectral sensitivities differ from a reference trichromat's, often reducing separation of long- and middle-wave signals. A shifted sensitivity, fewer receptors and loss of an entire independent class are different mechanisms and should not be conflated.

Color

Words: 35
Color vision OurBigBook.com
The perceived color of a transmitting sample depends on the illuminating spectrum and the wavelength-dependent transmission. Removing a blue band can make a sample appear yellow; absorption maximum alone does not determine a unique visual shade.

Microscopy

Words: 464 Articles: 16
Optics OurBigBook.com

X-ray microscopy

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Microscopy OurBigBook.com
Imaging with X-rays, combining suitable focusing or image-forming optics with contrast from absorption, phase or emitted signals. Photon-energy selection can make core-edge chemical contrast accessible, while achievable resolution depends on the optics, detector and measurement geometry.

Scanning transmission X-ray microscopy

Words: 50
X-ray microscopy OurBigBook.com
A focused X-ray probe scans a thin specimen while a detector records transmission. Scanning photon energy across an absorption edge adds local spectroscopic contrast, with spatial resolution set by the probe and scanning performance. Thickness and composition both affect transmission, so an energy stack and suitable references help distinguish them.

Scanning gate microscopy

Words: 43
Microscopy OurBigBook.com
A conducting scanning-probe tip acts as a movable electrostatic gate. Mapping conductance changes as the tip perturbs a quantum point contact or surrounding electron gas probes quantum transport. The image is a response to the tip, not automatically a noninvasive map of the unperturbed local current density.

Surface topography

Words: 20
Microscopy OurBigBook.com
The spatial height and shape of a surface. In atomic force microscopy, apparent lateral shape also depends on AFM tip convolution and the controller response.

Super-resolution microscopy

Words: 212 Articles: 5
Microscopy OurBigBook.com

Point accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Super-resolution microscopy OurBigBook.com
Transiently binding fluorescent probes provide spatially separated single-emitter observations whose fitted positions accumulate into a structural map. Probe exchange can replenish bleached emitters. Precision, specificity, event density, optical background and drift all affect the usable resolution; accumulating events does not itself remove systematic labelling error.
DNA-PAINT
Words: 29
Point accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography OurBigBook.com
Reversible complementary-strand recognition supplies transient fluorescent docking events on a DNA nanostructure. Individual events are localized and accumulated as in PAINT.[ref]

Photoactivated localization microscopy

Words: 138 Articles: 2
Super-resolution microscopy OurBigBook.com
PALM reconstructs a spatial map by activating sparse subsets of labels, estimating each isolated fluorophore's position and combining many frames. Optical resolution depends on localization uncertainty, labeling density, drift and linkage; repeatedly observing one label cannot recover unlabeled structures.
Sparse photoactivation
Words: 32
Photoactivated localization microscopy OurBigBook.com
A small subset of photoactivatable labels is fluorescent at any one time so that their overlapping point spread functions can usually be avoided. Repetition supplies many spatial localizations without requiring all labels to emit simultaneously.
Single-particle tracking PALM
Words: 70
Photoactivated localization microscopy OurBigBook.com
Sparse photoactivation allows successive positions of individual labelled molecules to be linked into trajectories; activation of fresh subsets yields many tracks in living cells. This extends photoactivated localization microscopy from accumulated positions to mobility. For free two-dimensional diffusion with independent per-coordinate fluorescence localization precision σ, instantaneous frames give mean squared displacement 4DΔt+4σ2. Motion blur, tracking errors, confinement and photobleaching must be accounted for before assigning mobility classes.[ref]

Optical resolution

Words: 103 Articles: 4
Microscopy OurBigBook.com

Diffraction bandwidth and detector pitch (p≤λf/(2D))

Words: 66
Optical resolution OurBigBook.com
For incoherent imaging with an unobstructed circular aperture of diameter D, the intensity-image spatial-frequency cutoff is D/(λf) in the focal plane. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem therefore gives the displayed pitch limit. The Rayleigh criterion instead gives a point-image separation 1.22λf/D. Consequently two samples per Rayleigh separation and sampling the full optical bandwidth differ by the factor 1.22. Neither sampling estimate guarantees useful contrast at arbitrarily low signal-to-noise ratio.

Diffraction limit

Words: 37
Optical resolution OurBigBook.com
The resolution scale imposed by a finite-aperture wave-imaging system under a stated criterion. For conventional optical microscopy, a common lateral scale is λ/(2NA). Changing the illumination, measured signal or reconstruction assumptions can change the applicable criterion.

Axial resolution

Optical resolution OurBigBook.com

Lateral resolution

Optical resolution OurBigBook.com

Optical sectioning

Microscopy OurBigBook.com

Ellipsometry

Words: 8
Optics OurBigBook.com
Measuring how specular reflection changes the polarization of an electromagnetic wave to infer optical properties.

Spatial resolution

Words: 48
Optics OurBigBook.com
The ability of an imaging or measurement system to distinguish nearby spatial features. A resolution criterion must specify the features and measurement conditions: diffraction, noise and sampling can all limit the distinction. A small pixel spacing alone does not establish high spatial resolution; electron microscope resolution illustrates the role of wavelength and numerical aperture.

Luminescence

Words: 80 Articles: 4
Optics OurBigBook.com
Light emission from excited matter that is not simply its thermal radiation at the local temperature. Fluorescence is one form of luminescence.

Electroluminescence

Words: 6
Luminescence OurBigBook.com
Light emission driven by an electric current or electric field.

Photoluminescence

Words: 33 Articles: 1
Luminescence OurBigBook.com
Emission of light following the absorption of photons.

Photoluminescence excitation spectrum

Electron optics studies how electric fields and magnetic fields guide electrons and form images. The Lorentz force supplies a trajectory description, while the de Broglie wavelength supplies the wave scale needed for diffraction. Both descriptions matter: steering a narrow beam and resolving two nearby specimen features are different achievements.
For a magnetic electron lens,
F=−ev×B,F⋅v=0.
(1)
Here e>0 is the elementary charge, v the electron velocity, and B the magnetic field. The second equality follows because a cross product is perpendicular to each factor: a static magnetic field bends the trajectory without increasing the kinetic energy. Acceleration instead requires work by an electric field. This distinction lets an electron microscope adjust imaging with magnetic fields while an accelerating voltage sets the electron momentum.

Transmission electron microscopy contrast is a difference in recorded signal between specimen regions under specified illumination, angular acceptance and detector settings. For a positive reference signal Sref​, one possible signed contrast convention is
C=Sref​S−Sref​​.
(2)

An objective aperture selects outgoing electron directions in the objective lens's back focal plane. Passing the central transmitted beam gives bright-field transmission electron microscopy; selecting a separated diffracted beam gives dark-field transmission electron microscopy.[ref]
In a paraxial approximation, an outgoing angle θ maps approximately to position r=fθ in this focal plane, where f is the objective focal length. A centred opening of radius a therefore admits ∣θ∣≲a/f. Selecting a direction selects a component of the outgoing wavefunction; the subsequent image still assigns intensity to specimen positions. The opening is not a hole cut into a real-space specimen image. Its angular selection must be distinguished from selecting a specimen region for electron diffraction.

Diffraction contrast
Words: 570 Articles: 3
Transmission electron microscopy contrast OurBigBook.com
Diffraction contrast is image-intensity variation caused by spatially varying electron diffraction conditions. JEOL documents a silicon semiconductor-interconnect specimen at 200kV: its differently oriented crystals are imaged in bright-field transmission electron microscopy and same-area dark-field transmission electron microscopy, alongside an electron diffraction pattern. Selecting the marked diffracted beam makes the corresponding crystal bright after it was dark. The preparation route, thickness and exposure are not supplied. The changed objective aperture selection provides a comparison within one specimen; the readout supports orientation-dependent contrast rather than a map of surface height or chemical composition.[ref]
This comparison is useful precisely because the material has not been replaced between the two images. It does not prove that thickness and chemical composition never influence transmission electron microscopy contrast. Instead, it supplies a concrete counterexample to assigning either quantity uniquely from brightness. A proposed extension is to repeat the first aperture setting after the second: recovery of the original contrast tests whether specimen motion or irradiation changed the comparison.

Lossless two-channel thickness scattering model (p0​=cos2(κt),pg​=sin2(κt))
Words: 377
Diffraction contrast OurBigBook.com
Consider an original illustrative model with exactly two outgoing scattering channels: a central beam 0 and one diffracted beam g. Let t≥0 be specimen thickness and κ>0 a constant coupling with units of inverse length. Normalize the probability amplitudes A0​,Ag​ to incident probability current, assume equal longitudinal speeds, and specify
dtdA0​​=iκAg​,dtdAg​​=iκA0​,A0​(0)=1,Ag​(0)=0.
(3)
These ordinary differential equations define a lossless toy model, not a fit to the silicon example or a complete theory of crystal scattering. Differentiating once more gives A0′′​=−κ2A0​, so
A0​=cos(κt),Ag​=isin(κt),p0​=∣A0​∣2=cos2(κt),pg​=∣Ag​∣2=sin2(κt).
(4)
The identity p0​+pg​=1 expresses conservation within these two scattering channels. Alternatively, substituting the ordinary differential equations into d(∣A0​∣2+∣Ag​∣2)/dt makes the two cross terms cancel. Here ideal bright-field transmission electron microscopy accepts fraction p0​ and rejects fraction pg​; ideal dark-field transmission electron microscopy accepts precisely the rejected channel. This complementarity requires the declared two-channel completeness and absence of loss.
Even with known κ, thickness is ambiguous: κt=π/4 and 3π/4 both give (p0​,pg​)=(1/2,1/2). Near t=0, pg​≃(κt)2; extending that approximation through a full oscillation would erase the ambiguity incorrectly. The model isolates reversible transfer between probability amplitudes; it does not say that every thicker specimen must look darker.
Real dark-field transmission electron microscopy usually collects only a subset of the directions rejected in bright-field transmission electron microscopy. Other elastic scattering directions, inelastic scattering and detector losses prevent a general two-image conservation rule. To keep loss and background separate, extend the counting model explicitly. Let ℓ be the fraction absent from both recorded beam channels, p0​+pg​=1 describe the remaining fraction, N be incident count per exposure, ηj​ the detector efficiency and bj​ its mean additive background. Then the expected value of recorded count nj​ is
E[nj​]=ηj​N(1−ℓ)pj​+bj​,j∈{0,g}.
(5)
For separately acquired equal-illumination exposures with known bj​,ηj​, the two corrected mean counts sum to N(1−ℓ), not necessarily N. Removal from these channels is not synonymous with physical absorption: an electron can leave the chosen acceptance or change kinetic energy without being stopped in the specimen. Background subtraction removes a mean offset, but its counting variance remains.
Transmission electron microscopy specimen dose and calibration
Words: 267
Transmission electron microscopy OurBigBook.com
JEOL's minimum-dose method focuses and corrects astigmatism away from the recording position before exposing it, reducing irradiation of the chosen field.[ref] A downstream objective aperture cannot undo irradiation that has already reached the specimen: rejecting more outgoing electrons does not itself reduce specimen exposure.
For an original dose budget, define D as incident electron count per specimen area, rather than absorbed energy per mass. A uniform beam of electric current magnitude I, illuminating area A for time T, gives
N=eIT​,D=eAIT​,
(6)
where e is the elementary charge. Choosing I=1pA, T=1s and A=1μm2 gives approximately 6.24×106 incident electrons, or 6.24electronsnm−2. This is an invented exposure calculation, not a safe-dose recommendation. Focusing and searching exposures must also enter the accumulated budget.
If detected counts follow a Poisson distribution, a mean count μ has standard deviation μ​. Ignoring background, 100 accepted counts therefore have 10% relative counting uncertainty, while 25 have 20%. Reducing accepted counts can reveal useful diffraction contrast while increasing counting uncertainty. It is useful to specify both contrast and count budget when discussing electron microscope resolution.
A proposed measurement calibration sequence records a beam-blocked detector background, an illuminated empty support region, and a specimen image with fixed voltage, exposure and detector gain. Test detector linearity with exposure time before comparing corrected intensities. Calibrate the image scale against a known spacing, as in microscope scale calibration, and independently calibrate electron diffraction spacing at its own lens settings; one calibration does not supply the other. Register compared regions, record objective aperture selection, specimen tilt and accumulated exposure, then repeat the first setting to test drift and irradiation changes. These are proposed controls, not undocumented steps attributed to JEOL's silicon example.

Electron microscope OurBigBook.com
A scanning electron microscope scans a focused electron probe across a specimen and assigns a detector signal to each probe position. Secondary electrons leaving the irradiated region often reveal surface relief; backscattered electrons can provide composition-dependent contrast. Image brightness records the selected signal, rather than a transmitted projection enlarged by two lenses. Display enlargement is therefore set by the ratio of display width to scanned specimen width. Surface geometry and composition both affect brightness.[ref]

Early two-stage electron microscope experiment

Words: 225
Electron microscope OurBigBook.com
Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed electron optics while improving the writing spot of a cathode-ray oscilloscope.[ref] A structured object tests image formation more strongly than a single bright spot: each feature must retain its own image position.
On 7 April 1931, a cold cathode source and two short magnetic coils imaged aperture grids at 50kV. A platinum grid preceded the first coil; a bronze grid preceded the second. The fluorescent screen showed one-stage grid images and the first grid reimaged through both stages. Comparing these patterns tested successive image formation, not merely beam concentration. Heating could destroy even metal grids. This prototype did not establish resolution beyond an optical microscope.[ref]
In 1933, Ruska measured 3mm focal lengths at 75kV with a pole-piece lens, then built an instrument giving 12000-fold magnification.[ref] TU Berlin dates images surpassing conventional optical microscope resolution to 1933.[ref]
A fluorescent screen converts the spatial electron distribution into visible light.[ref] A collector reporting only total electric current would discard that spatial pattern. In a two-stage image relay, the first lens makes an intermediate real image; the second treats that image as its object. The diagram below illustrates this geometry with invented distances and an ideal beam.

Two-stage electron imaging (m=m1​m2​)

Words: 315
Electron microscope OurBigBook.com
Consider two ideal thin electron lenses in successive imaging stages. In each stage choose positive object and image distances ui​,vi​ for a real image, measured from its effective lens plane, and neglect the image rotation of a magnetic electron lens. The paraxial approximation gives
fi​1​=ui​1​+vi​1​,mi​=−ui​vi​​,m=m1​m2​.
(7)
The product follows directly by writing y1​=m1​y0​ and y2​=m2​y1​. Here mi​ is transverse magnification, rather than the enlargement applied later to a photograph. Both inversions cancel in this planar model; actual magnetic electron lenses can additionally rotate the image.
For an original worked example, take u1​=40mm, v1​=80mm, u2​=50mm and v2​=150mm. Then
f1​=380​mm,f2​=37.5mm,m1​=−2,m2​=−3,m=6.
(8)
A 100μm object interval becomes 600μm at the screen. The second lens sits v1​+u2​=130mm after the first. These are calculated distances, not measurements of the 1931 instrument.
To measure magnification, divide a screen interval between corresponding grid features by the independently known object interval. Repeat over several periods to reduce endpoint uncertainty. For a proposed check, record accelerating voltage, lens electric currents, screen position and specimen orientation; compare one-stage and two-stage images, refocusing as necessary. Changing a lens electric current should change focus and scale, while a blank exposure checks detector background. Keep irradiation and recording enlargement controlled, and repeat the original setting to test drift or specimen damage. These are suggested checks, not a claim that every check was performed in 1931. A grid-scale measurement establishes magnification; resolving much finer features requires a separate target and contrast criterion.

Electron microscope resolution

Words: 386
Electron microscope OurBigBook.com
Electron microscope resolution concerns distinguishable specimen detail under a specified contrast criterion. It depends on diffraction, lens defects, electron energy spread, specimen motion and detection. A smaller de Broglie wavelength permits finer detail in principle, but neither wavelength nor magnification is the instrument's measured resolution.
For an electron accelerated from negligible initial kinetic energy through a positive electric potential difference U, combine K=eU, the relativistic energy-momentum relation and the de Broglie wavelength:
p2c2=K(K+2me​c2),λ(U)=2me​eU(1+2me​c2eU​)​h​.
(9)
Here h is the Planck constant, me​ the electron mass, e the elementary charge, and c the speed of light. This includes the relativistic correction omitted by the low-voltage electron accelerating-voltage wavelength approximation. With me​≃9.1093837×10−31kg and SI defining values of h,e,c, calculated wavelengths are approximately 6.979, 3.701 and 1.969pm at 30, 100 and 300kV respectively. The rounded mass agrees with the recommended value.[ref]
For a circular aperture admitting a small semi-angle α, the Rayleigh criterion suggests a diffraction-limited resolution scale dD​=0.61λ/α. At 100kV and α=10mrad, this gives 0.226nm, already much larger than the 0.00370nm wavelength. This is an ideal aperture estimate. Transmission electron microscopy with coherent illumination and a particular specimen requires its own image-contrast analysis; this scale alone is not a universal two-feature resolution test.
An original illustrative blur model adds competing effects:
b(α)2=(α0.61λ​)2+(Cs​α3)2+(Cc​αKΔK​)2+b02​.
(10)
Define Cs​α3 as a characteristic transverse blur from the electron-lens analogue of spherical aberration, and Cc​αΔK/K as one from energy-dependent focusing, the analogue of chromatic aberration. The coefficients Cs​,Cc​ have units of length, ΔK is a chosen characteristic kinetic energy spread, and b0​ is a fixed residual blur. Adding their squares is a declared heuristic, not a measured point spread function or a rigorous resolution theorem. The model omits contrast transfer, specimen scattering and signal statistics, so its minimum is only an estimate within its assumptions.
Choose Cs​=Cc​=1mm, ΔK=0.7eV and b0​=0.10nm at K=100keV. At 5mrad, the four contributions are about 0.452, 0.125, 0.035 and 0.100nm, giving b≃0.480nm. At 10mrad, the diffraction contribution falls to 0.226nm but the assumed spherical aberration contribution grows to 1.00nm. Thus opening the aperture indefinitely worsens this model's image. All these values are calculations with chosen parameters, not observations of any microscope.

Electron lens

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Electron optics OurBigBook.com
An electron lens uses an electric field or magnetic field to make trajectories from an object point converge towards an image point. It has no glass for the electrons to pass through. In a paraxial approximation, an effective focal length permits the same first-order image geometry used for a thin lens; finite beam angles, energy spread and misalignment limit this approximation.

Magnetic electron lens

Words: 83
Electron lens OurBigBook.com
A magnetic electron lens uses a solenoid around the beam axis; iron pole pieces concentrate its magnetic field.[ref] A strictly axial trajectory in a perfectly uniform axial magnetic field experiences no Lorentz force, since v×B=0. Near the entrance, a radial field component turns an advancing electron azimuthally; the resulting sideways velocity in the axial magnetic field also produces a radial Lorentz force. This couples image rotation and focusing. Real trajectories bend smoothly, whereas a thin lens diagram compresses that bending into one effective plane.

Photometry (optics)

Words: 1k Articles: 17
Optics OurBigBook.com
Photometry weights visible electromagnetic radiation by standardized visual response functions; radiometry measures its energy and power without visual weighting.[ref]
The question is how much light a source supplies under a stated visual weighting. A beam containing 1mW at the defining frequency 540THz has luminous flux 0.683lm. Moving the same radiant flux to a region of smaller spectral luminous efficacy reduces its luminous flux. Changing the optical spectrum changes this conversion even when its total power stays fixed. This makes photometry useful for comparing lighting, while radiometry remains necessary for an energy budget. The lumen counts luminous flux; the candela additionally specifies its distribution over solid angle.
Two measurement routes implement the weighting: measure an optical spectrum and evaluate a weighted integral, or use a photometer whose spectral responsivity approximates the prescribed weighting. Both require a specified collection geometry. Neither is a complete prediction of an individual's perception of a scene.[ref]

The wavelength coordinate is in standard air, rather than vacuum; changing coordinates requires converting the spectral radiant flux density as well. The official prescription uses linear interpolation between the specified 1 nm entries.[ref]
Write λa​ for the standard-air wavelength at 540THz. With spectral radiant flux Φe,λ​ in Wnm−1 and dλ in nanometres, the luminous flux is
Φv​=Km​∫360nm830nm​V(λ)Φe,λ​(λ)dλ,Km​=V(λa​)Kcd​​,Kcd​=683lmW−1.
(11)
The integral has units of watts, and Km​ converts them to lumens. For radiation at a single wavelength λ0​ with total radiant flux P, this reduces to Φv​=Km​V(λ0​)P. For a sufficiently narrow finite band, this is an approximation requiring nearly constant V across the band.[ref]

A monochromator supplies a small beam; scanning wavelength yields spectral responsivity, and scanning position checks response across the aperture. Finite spectral bandwidth requires correction. On the photometric bench (§§3.4.1, 3.5.3, 3.5.6), align lamp and aperture reference planes, set the lamp's electric current, stabilize, and compare a check lamp with standard photometers. The readout is a voltmeter signal. Subtract the shutter-closed reading (§3.4.4), divide by converter gain to infer electric current, and use calibrated illuminance responsivity SA​ to obtain Ev​=i/SA​. For a distant source, luminous intensity follows from Iv​=Ev​d2, with d between reference planes.
Controls include repeat lamp operations, distance changes to test the inverse-square law, temperature corrections and gain linearity checks. Spectral mismatch correction is source dependent (§3.4.3). Unknown optical spectra, spatial nonuniformity and incorrect reference planes remain limitations.[ref]

Lambertian reflectance

Words: 181 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Lambertian reflectance is the ideal diffuse-reflection model with direction-independent outgoing radiance, the frequency-integrated specific intensity. If a fraction 0≤ρ≤1 of incident radiant flux is reflected, a surface receiving irradiance E has reflected radiance L=ρE/π. The reflected outward power per area is πL=ρE by the same hemispherical integral used for radiant exitance. Its radiant intensity still acquires the projected area factor in Lambert's cosine law.
For E=100Wm−2 and ρ=0.80, the reflected radiance is 80/π≈25.4648Wm−2sr−1. A patch of area 0.020m2 reflects 1.6W in total, and its radiant intensities at 0∘ and 60∘ are respectively 1.6/π and 0.8/πWsr−1. The radiance stays fixed as the view changes, provided the illumination stays fixed. Changing the incident angle can change irradiance and therefore the reflected radiance.

Lambertian reflectance OurBigBook.com
A spherical body of radius R observed from distance d≫R is illuminated and viewed from the same direction, with incident irradiance F⋆​. For uniform Lambertian reflectance A, a patch at angle θ has outgoing radiance AF⋆​cosθ/π. The observer receives this radiance times projected area divided by d2. Since ∫hemisphere​cos2θdS=2πR2/3, integration proves the displayed full-phase irradiance. Its geometric albedo is 2A/3. Total reflected power alone does not specify the brightness in one direction for a non-Lambertian surface.

Lambert's cosine law (I(θ)=I(0)cosθ)

Words: 136
Optics OurBigBook.com
For an ideal diffuse emitting or reflecting planar surface with uniform direction-independent radiance, the radiant intensity in a direction at angle θ to its unit normal is I(θ)=I(0)cosθ. This follows immediately from I=LAcosθ and the projected area formula. The worked radiance example and diagram show the 0∘ and 60∘ cases. Lambertian reflectance supplies one physical idealization realizing the law; an ideal blackbody provides an emitting example.
The historical setting is Johann Heinrich Lambert's Photometria sive de mensura et gradibus luminis, colorum et umbrae, published in Augsburg in 1760. Its Part I, §139, explicitly compares normal and oblique illumination using the sine of the source's elevation, equivalently the cosine of its angle from the receiving normal vector. This is an early receiving-surface projection calculation; the modern outgoing-patch statement above keeps radiance, radiant intensity and irradiance distinct. [ref] [ref].

Recoil energy OurBigBook.com
Absorption of momentum p followed by emission of p′ changes a free atom's momentum by p−p′. For isotropic emission of fixed magnitude, its mean vector is zero. The energy change then separates into a directional work term and two positive recoil terms. If absorption directions are also isotropic and uncorrelated with the initial momentum, the work term averages away. Equal incoming and outgoing photon magnitudes give two recoil energies per cycle.

Refraction

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Optics OurBigBook.com
Refraction changes the direction of a transmitted wave when it crosses between media with different phase velocities. For light at a planar interface, Snell's law relates the angles measured from the normal vector through the refractive indices. At normal incidence the direction remains unchanged even though the wavelength and phase velocity can change. The worked example under geometrical optics distinguishes transmission from total internal reflection.
For light, refraction explains why a submerged object looks nearer the surface and why an optical lens can form an image. A wavefront crossing a boundary must retain a consistent wave phase along that boundary: its normal spacing changes with phase velocity, and oblique light rays change direction. Normal incidence separates these two effects especially clearly.
Take stationary, transparent, homogeneous media with isotropy, linearity of their optical response, and real positive refractive indices, at one chosen frequency f. With c the vacuum speed of light and λ0​=c/f the vacuum wavelength, medium j has
nj​=vphase,j​c​,vphase,j​=fλj​,λj​=nj​λ0​​,kj​=λj​2π​=cnj​ω​,ω=2πf.
(15)
The frequency is unchanged at a stationary boundary; the phase velocity, wavelength and wavenumber can change. Here nj​ is a phase refractive index, not the group refractive index. If there is optical dispersion, evaluate nj​ at this same frequency on both sides.[ref]
For an original idealized air–water example, stipulate na​=1 and nw​=4/3, with vacuum wavelength 600nm. Then f=c/(600nm)≈4.99654×1014Hz, the water phase velocity is 3c/4, and its wavelength is 450nm. At an air angle of incidence 30∘, Snell's law gives a water angle of refraction arcsin(3/8)≈22.0243∘. These stipulated values illustrate the relations; actual refractive indices depend on material conditions and frequency. By reversibility of an optical ray, the same path emerging from water has outgoing air angle 30∘.

With incident light travelling to the right, use positive object distance u to the left, image distance d to the right, and curvature radius R toward a right-hand centre. For a ray hitting at small height Y, its incoming inclination, outgoing downward inclination and inward-normal downward inclination are α≃Y/u, β≃Y/d and θ≃Y/R. The paraxial approximation to Snell's law gives n1​(α+θ)=n2​(θ−β). Cancelling Y proves the title equation. Virtual conjugates and other centre orientations require corresponding signed distances. Applying the relation at both faces of a thin lens proves the lensmaker's equation.

The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident light ray and the line of the surface normal vector at the point of incidence. Use the acute angle on the incident side, with 0≤θi​<90∘ for a nongrazing incident light ray. An angle measured from the surface itself is its complement 90∘−θi​. Refraction OurBigBook.com
The angle of refraction is the angle between the transmitted light ray and the surface normal vector, measured on the transmitted side. With positive refractive indices, a propagating transmitted light ray satisfies ni​sinθi​=nt​sinθt​ in Snell's law. The incident and transmitted angles are measured from the same normal line, not from the surface and not from the emergent light ray at a second surface.

Normal incidence (θi​=0)

Words: 58
Refraction OurBigBook.com
At normal incidence, the incident light ray follows the surface normal vector. Snell's law gives θt​=0 for positive refractive indices, so the transmitted light ray does not bend. Nevertheless, its phase velocity and wavelength change if the refractive index changes. A single axial light ray therefore cannot measure apparent depth: neighboring light rays and their directions supply that information. A reflected component can still be present; no bending of the transmitted light ray does not imply complete transmission.

Interface phase matching (ki,∥​=kt,∥​)

Words: 214
Refraction OurBigBook.com
At a stationary, uniform planar boundary, incident and transmitted plane waves have the same variation of wave phase along the interface and in time. The figure marks places where equal-wave phase wavefronts meet the boundary. Although their perpendicular spacing differs, their intersections must advance along the boundary together. This is the local mechanism behind Snell's law.[ref]
For a short derivation, let x run along the interface and z increase into the transmitted medium. Write each wave phase as Φj​=kj,x​x+kj,z​z−ωj​t+ϕj​. The electromagnetic boundary conditions must hold at every x,t on z=0; their matching requires ωi​=ωt​ and ki,x​=kt,x​. Constant offsets ϕj​ and wave amplitudes are determined separately. Since kj,x​=kj​sinθj​, this gives
cni​ω​sinθi​=cnt​ω​sinθt​.
(16)
For nonzero tangential wavenumber, the spacing of equal-wave phase intersections along the interface is λi​/sinθi​=λt​/sinθt​. It is not the perpendicular wavelength. At normal incidence, the tangential wavenumber vanishes and the interface is uniform in wave phase.[ref]

Refraction OurBigBook.com
A submerged object looks shallower because its emerging light rays bend away from the surface normal vector. Their backward extensions give an approximate virtual image nearer the surface. A light ray reaches the boundary at (x,0), with object-side angle θobj​ and observer-side angle θobs​, both measured from the upward normal vector. For x>0, its backward extension meets the object's normal line x=0 at z=−daxis​, where
x=dtanθobj​,nobj​sinθobj​=nobs​sinθobs​,daxis​=tanθobs​x​=dnobj​cosθobj​nobs​cosθobs​​.
(17)
This axis-intercept depth is exact for that one transmitted light ray in the stated model. It tends to dpar​ as the angles tend to zero; at exactly zero the quotient is interpreted as a limit. These elementary tangent, sine and cosine relations show precisely where the small-angle approximation enters.

Measuring refraction with a rectangular block

Words: 238
Refraction OurBigBook.com
Use a slit light source, a rectangular transparent block on plain paper, pencil, ruler and protractor. Trace the block outline, keep it fixed, and mark widely separated points on incident and emergent light rays. Remove the block and join the entry and exit points to reconstruct its internal light ray. Draw the surface normal vector at entry; measure i outside and r inside from that normal line. Choose a path exiting the opposite parallel face rather than a side edge. Repeat for a range of i with the same block and source colour; record i,r,sini,sinr and repeat-reading spread. Plot sini vertically against sinr horizontally: Snell's law predicts slope nblock​/nair​, approximately the block's refractive index. The emergent light ray should be parallel to the incident one. Beam width, pencil marks, protractor resolution, block movement and colour spread limit precision; a narrow-colour source reduces spread from optical dispersion. These are measured angular readings, not a direct timing of phase velocity.[ref]
A normal incidence trial checks the drawn normal and the absence of bending, but the ratio sini/sinr is then 0/0. Small nonzero angles also make that ratio sensitive to reading errors. Compare several trials through the slope rather than relying on one nearly axial pair. This rectangular-block measurement complements the existing total internal reflection experiment, which probes a different boundary condition.

Image formation

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Optics OurBigBook.com
Image formation assigns each object point a corresponding image point: outgoing light rays from that object point either converge there, giving a real image, or diverge as though they originated there, giving a virtual image. The requirement applies separately to each point. Bringing unrelated light rays together makes a bright patch, but does not preserve the object's pattern. This point-by-point correspondence explains how an optical camera records a scene. [ref].
Use the same convention as thin lens: place the optical lens at x=0, with incident light travelling to the right and a real object at x=−u, u>0. Write the image coordinate as x=v, so v>0 for a real image and v<0 for a virtual image. Heights ho​,hi​ are positive above the optical axis and negative below it. In air, within the paraxial approximation, a thin lens obeys
u1​+v1​=f1​,v=u−ffu​,m=ho​hi​​=−uv​.
(18)
Here f is the signed focal length, positive for a converging optical lens and negative for a diverging optical lens; the expression for v assumes u=f. Object distance u is positive even though the object's coordinate is negative. These coordinate rules describe transmission through the optical lens; a mirror reverses the outgoing direction, so do not identify its image distance with this same rightward coordinate. [ref].
The beauty of geometrical optics is that two convenient light rays can locate a point, while a whole admitted bundle forms its image. For a converging thin lens, an incident light ray parallel to the optical axis exits through the rear optical focus; a light ray through the centre continues undeviated. Real optical lens elements do not focus every admitted light ray exactly: optical aberrations and diffraction limit the point correspondence. The diagrams below are original ideal-model constructions, not measured data. [ref].

The near point is the closest position at which an eye can focus comfortably by accommodation. Its distance D is measured from the eye and depends on the observer. The conventional textbook reference D=250mm is an assumption, not a universal anatomical constant. Angular magnification of a magnifying glass is usually referred to unaided viewing of the same object at this distance.

Conjugate optical plane

Words: 54
Image formation OurBigBook.com
Two conjugate optical planes are object and image planes related by an imaging system: points in one are imaged onto corresponding points in the other in the paraxial approximation. For a converging thin lens forming a real image in air, their distances u,v>0 obey 1/u+1/v=1/f. Exchanging u and v preserves this relation; this symmetry gives the two settings of the Bessel lens displacement method.

An optical bench is a rail or aligned platform carrying an object, optical lens elements and a screen or detector at readable positions. It turns image formation into measurements of position and transverse magnification. Read distances between the optical planes rather than arbitrary holder boundaries; keep heights and optical axis alignment controlled. [ref].

Real image

Words: 545
Image formation OurBigBook.com
A real image lies where the outgoing light rays from each object point actually intersect in geometrical optics. A screen or detector placed at that image plane receives the focused pattern. The screen reveals the real image; it does not create the intersection. A viewer can also see a real image without a screen if their eye receives the diverging light rays beyond the intersection. [ref].
For a converging thin lens and real object with u>f>0, the real image has v>0 and signed transverse magnification m<0. Inversion is a property of this particular setup, not the definition of a real image. With f=10cm and ho​=0.50cm, the following are predictions:
Object distance uImage distance vTransverse magnification mSigned image height hi​
30cm15cm−1/2−0.25cm
20cm20cm−1−0.50cm
15cm30cm−2−1.00cm
To test both image position and transverse magnification, use an optical bench with an illuminated arrow or millimetre target, a converging optical lens of nominal focal length 10cm, a movable white screen and a ruler. Measure corresponding target and image intervals, rather than guessing the whole image size when it exceeds the screen. PASCO's Experiment 12 compares distance-based and size-based magnification; the following procedure uses several object distances, as in the Northern Virginia laboratory. [ref]; [ref].
  • Align target centre, optical lens centre and screen along one optical axis, with target and screen perpendicular to it. Record bench positions of the actual target plane, optical lens plane and screen surface; distances between holder edges introduce an offset.
  • Start at u=30cm. Move the screen through the expected v=15cm region until the target's central detail is sharpest. Record u, measured v, the corresponding target and image intervals, and whether the arrow is inverted. Give the measured size ratio a negative sign if inverted.
  • Repeat at u=20cm and u=15cm. Compare the measured signed size ratio with −v/u, and calculate fest​=uv/(u+v) for each pair. The three ideal rows above are predictions to compare against, not entries to copy into the measurement record. [ref].
Keep the optical lens, illumination and central target detail fixed between trials. Approach best focus from both sides and record the interval over which sharpness is difficult to distinguish; repeat focusing to estimate its reproducibility. A modest central aperture stop tests whether peripheral light rays change the result, but also reduces brightness. Spherical aberration, chromatic aberration and diffraction can broaden the optimum; a thick optical lens also makes the chosen reference plane imperfect. Treat nominal f as an initial prediction, and report position and interval-reading limits instead of forcing exact agreement. [ref].
Moving the object toward the front optical focus from outside makes the real image larger and farther away. A failed screen search near u=f can therefore mean that the real image is beyond the bench, rather than that a virtual image has formed. At exactly u=f, the outgoing bundle from each point is parallel and no finite screen position focuses it.

Virtual image

Words: 660 Articles: 1
Image formation OurBigBook.com
A virtual image is the apparent origin of an outgoing diverging bundle: the backward extensions of its light rays intersect at the image point. Those extensions are geometric constructions, not backward-travelling light. A screen placed there cannot intercept the outgoing bundle to display that virtual image. An eye or a second optical lens receiving the actual outgoing light rays can nevertheless form a subsequent real image. “Virtual” describes this imaging stage, not whether the image can be seen or photographed. [ref].
For a converging thin lens with 0<u<f, the same equations give v<0 and m=f/(f−u)>1: the virtual image is upright and enlarged. For the illustrative choice f=10cm, u=7.5cm, ho​=0.30cm,
v=−30cm,m=4,hi​=1.20cm.
(19)
The image appears farther from the optical lens than the object. A diverging thin lens with a real object instead has v<0 and 0<m<1, so a virtual image need not be enlarged. A plane mirror provides another virtual image, located behind the reflecting surface by backward extensions of the reflected light rays. [ref].
For a direct viewing test, bring the target to u=7.5cm, search for a sharp screen image on the outgoing side, then remove the screen and look through the optical lens toward the target. Expect an upright enlarged view if the eye receives the bundle and can focus. Record the eye position: 5cm beyond the optical lens gives a predicted apparent distance 35cm. This adapts the Northern Virginia laboratory's comparison. [ref].
For a position measurement, use parallax localization of a virtual image. Place a movable pencil tip or narrow comparison marker beside the apparent image, and view that marker directly beside or above the optical lens, while viewing the image through it. Move the head a little sideways and move the marker along the bench until relative lateral motion vanishes. Read its coordinate xm​; the estimate is v=xm​<0. Deliberately place the marker nearer and farther to check that relative motion reverses on opposite sides of the match. This follows Orhan Aytür's lens laboratory, which uses a pencil to locate a virtual image. [ref].
Keep target and optical lens fixed, use one eye and the central image detail, and ensure the marker itself is not viewed through the optical lens. A marker blocked by the target, or a head movement that loses the bundle through the aperture, invalidates that trial. Repeat the match from both directions and record its depth range. This measures apparent depth; comparing apparent sizes at different depths does not directly measure transverse magnification. Near u=f, apparent depth becomes very large and the match is poorly constrained. A failed screen search alone therefore needs the distance check and the viewing test.

Parallax localization of a virtual image

Words: 133
Virtual image OurBigBook.com
Parallax localization of a virtual image matches the apparent depth of a virtual image to a directly viewed physical marker. A sideways change of viewpoint changes their relative apparent positions if their depths differ. Adjust the marker until that relative motion vanishes, and use its coordinate to estimate image position. The marker must be viewed directly; viewing it through the same optical lens compares two images rather than an image and a known physical depth. [ref].
For two nearly aligned points at distances Li​,Lm​ from an eye displaced sideways by δ, the small-angle approximation gives a change of relative viewing angle proportional to δ(1/Li​−1/Lm​). It vanishes when Li​=Lm​, and changes sign across that match. When both distances are large, the difference is small, explaining the poor depth precision near the thin lens condition u=f.

Magnification

Words: 666 Articles: 2
Image formation OurBigBook.com
Magnification compares an image's scale with a specified reference. Transverse magnification compares signed lengths in object and image planes; angular magnification compares viewing angles at an observer. Both are dimensionless quantities, but they answer different questions. A projected real image twice as tall has ∣m∣=2; an optical telescope's advertised viewing enlargement normally concerns angular magnification. [ref].
Always specify the sign and the reference arrangement. For signed transverse magnification, m<0 means inverted and m>0 means upright; ∣m∣>1 means enlarged and 0<∣m∣<1 means reduced. A larger virtual image can subtend a modest viewing angle if it is farther away. At u=f, an ideal converging thin lens has no finite image height and hence no finite transverse magnification, while angular magnification can remain finite. Enlargement also does not guarantee extra detail: diffraction-limited resolution and optical aberrations limit the information available to enlarge. [ref].

Transverse magnification (m=hi​/ho​)

Words: 240
Magnification OurBigBook.com
Transverse magnification is the ratio of corresponding signed lengths perpendicular to the optical axis. For an ideal image of a small arrow of nonzero height,
m=ho​hi​​.
(20)
Use the same upward-positive height convention in both planes. Thus an upright 0.50cm arrow imaged as −0.25cm has m=−1/2: inverted and half as tall. The sign describes orientation; real image versus virtual image describes ray intersections. They are separate properties, even when a particular thin lens setup correlates them.[ref]
For a thin lens with object coordinate −u and image coordinate v, the undeviated centre light ray is the straight line through (−u,ho​) and (0,0), so its height at x=v is hi​=−ho​v/u. This is the signed similar triangles argument. Combining it with the thin lens equation gives
m=−uv​=−u−ff​(u=f).
(21)
For f>0, u>2f gives −1<m<0; u=2f gives m=−1; f<u<2f gives m<−1; and 0<u<f gives m>1. At u=f, the image is conventionally “at infinity”: the divergent expressions for v and m describe the limiting behaviour, not a finite image of infinite height. Different object points produce parallel bundles in different directions, which is why angular magnification remains meaningful.
The real image experiment tests m in two independent ways: signed ratios of measured corresponding intervals, and −v/u from measured longitudinal distances. As a further prediction, moving from u=30cm to u=15cm for f=10cm swaps u,v, changing m=−1/2 to m=−2. The two image sizes differ by a factor of four, while both images remain inverted. This reversal follows from the symmetric thin lens equation and connects to the Bessel lens displacement method.

Angular magnification is the ratio of the signed viewing angle with an optical instrument to the signed viewing angle in a stated reference arrangement. Measure both as apparent directions from the eye, positive toward the same side of the optical axis; then an inverted view has negative Mθ​. Specular reflection (r=i−2(i⋅n)n)

Words: 294 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
At a smooth mirror with unit normal vector n, an incoming unit direction i has outgoing direction i−2(i⋅n)n. Thus the incident and reflected rays make equal angles with the normal.
More precisely, specular reflection redirects each incident light ray into the direction prescribed by the law of reflection, rather than spreading it over many outgoing directions. The incident light ray, reflected light ray, and local normal vector lie in one plane. The surface must be sufficiently smooth on the scale of the wavelength for this model to describe its reflected beam; a visibly flat surface can still scatter light if its microscopic roughness is appreciable. [ref].
The displayed formula uses unit vectors i,n,r and the dot product. It preserves the component parallel to the mirror and reverses the normal component. For a mirror along y=0, take n=(0,1) and i=(3/5,−4/5). Then i⋅n=−4/5 and r=(3/5,4/5): both directions have vector norm one, and both make an angle arccos(4/5)≈36.87∘ with the relevant normal direction. Replacing n by −n leaves the result unchanged.
This same local rule explains a flat mirror's virtual image. For a source at (0,a) above y=0, backward extensions of reflected light rays intersect at (0,−a). The light remains above the mirror; its apparent origin lies below it. A curved mirror changes its normal vector from point to point and can instead make reflected light rays converge. The geometry of image formation therefore starts with one simple direction rule. [ref].

Optical tweezers

Words: 4k Articles: 23
Optics OurBigBook.com
Optical tweezers hold and move a small particle using the force exerted by a tightly focused beam of light, usually from a laser. They can position transparent beads in a liquid and manipulate suitable biological cells. Attaching a molecule to a trapped bead turns the bead into a handle: a measured bead displacement, together with a calibrated spring constant, reveals the force exerted on the attachment. This makes microscopic manipulation and measurement possible without a mechanical tool touching the bead. Living biological cells were manipulated with infrared beams by Ashkin, Dziedzic and Yamane in 1987; Svoboda and Block used trapped beads to measure forces from individual molecules in 1994. [ref] [ref].
Why can light pull a bead towards a focus? Light carries momentum. A transparent bead with a higher refractive index than the surrounding liquid bends transmitted light rays by refraction, changing their momentum; conservation of momentum requires an opposite transfer to the bead. In the geometrical optics picture, unequal illumination of a displaced bead produces a net restoring force towards the brighter region. For a particle much smaller than the wavelength, a physical optics description replaces that ray picture. The detailed force depends on particle size, refractive index, beam shape and wavelength; the qualitative attraction does not supply a universal formula for every particle.
The optical gradient force draws a suitable transparent bead towards high illumination, while the optical scattering force generally pushes along beam propagation. A stable three-dimensional optical trap needs a balance with a restoring force in each direction: transverse confinement alone does not ensure axial confinement. Strong focusing can make the backward axial gradient contribution large enough to balance the forward scattering contribution, with the equilibrium displaced from the focus. Higher refractive index alone is insufficient; absorbing particles, different index contrasts and different beam geometries can behave differently. [ref].
Historically, Ashkin's 1970 experiments accelerated and trapped particles using radiation pressure. The 1986 paper by Ashkin, Dziedzic, Bjorkholm and Chu demonstrated the single-beam gradient optical trap for transparent particles. These are distinct steps: the earlier work established optical manipulation, and the later work supplied the tightly focused single-beam arrangement. [ref] [ref].
Near a stable equilibrium, a harmonic optical trap behaves like a spring; thermal calibration of an optical trap uses its Brownian motion to determine the effective spring constant. The later passage through a translating optical trap sections instead consider a moving localized potential energy, which need not remain harmonic throughout a passage.

This determines stiffness only after removing detector noise and accounting for drift, exposure averaging and finite bandwidth. Position variance does not supply a force calibration if the coordinate scale is unknown.

Ashkin radiation-pressure trapping experiment

Words: 149
Optical tweezers OurBigBook.com
Arthur Ashkin's 1970 first experiment suspended transparent latex spheres in water inside a 120μm glass cell. A horizontal 514.5nm argon laser beam, focused to a 6.2μm radius, illuminated individual beads viewed through a microscope. An off-centre 2.68μm bead moved toward the beam axis and downstream until reaching the cell wall; blocking the beam released it into Brownian motion. Transparent particles and liquid reduced competing thermal effects. This observed sequence separates transverse attraction from downstream radiation pressure: wall-assisted confinement is not free three-dimensional confinement by one beam.[ref]
The beam-blocking comparison is particularly informative: persistence against a wall while illuminated and release when illumination stops test an optical cause. To infer a force from the downstream velocity, one additionally needs a linear drag model and the bead's distance from the wall; the observed motion alone does not calibrate an unrestricted harmonic optical trap.

In 1986, Arthur Ashkin, Joseph Martin Dziedzic, John Ernst Bjorkholm and Steven Chu used spatially filtered 514.5nm argon laser light, a water-immersion objective of numerical aperture 1.25, and a water-filled glass cell. An auxiliary beam loaded large glass beads; dispersed small particles entered by Brownian motion. A side microscope and 90∘ scattering of light detector provided readout. Their Fig. 1 shows a 10μm bead below the focus with about 100mW. On p. 290, silica size was inferred by scattering against a latex standard; translating the cell imposed fluid drag. These observations support single-beam confinement, while inferred size depends on the scattering model.[ref]
A loading beam can help bring a bead into the capture region without supplying its subsequent confinement. Distinguish loading, holding and sensing when interpreting an apparatus drawing. The following optical trap position readout is a proposed calibration arrangement; its detector layout is not a reconstruction of this historical experiment.

An optical gradient force arises from spatial variation in illumination. In a usual optical trap for a suitable transparent particle with higher refractive index than its surroundings, it draws the particle towards high light intensity. It supplies a restoring force near a stable trap, but three-dimensional confinement also depends on the optical scattering force. The direction and size depend on the particle and field; attraction to the brightest point is not universal. [ref].

The geometrical optics account of an optical trap adds the momentum flux changes of refracted and reflected light rays. It applies when the bead is large compared with the surrounding medium's wavelength. When the bead is much smaller, an induced electric dipole gives a different approximation. For a homogeneous dielectric sphere of radius a, define p(t)=Re[αE0​e−iωt], with E0​ the peak complex electric field and α its SI polarizability. In a transparent, nonmagnetic, nondispersive host,
ϵm​=ϵ0​nm2​,α=4πϵm​a3np2​+2nm2​np2​−nm2​​,I=21​nm​ϵ0​c∣E0​∣2,
(23)
where np​,nm​ are particle and host refractive indices, I is cycle-averaged light intensity, ϵ0​ is the vacuum permittivity and c is the speed of light. The quasistatic electric dipole approximation requires 2πnm​a/λ0​≪1, with λ0​ the vacuum wavelength, and a field nearly uniform across the bead.
For real quasistatic α, building an induced electric dipole gives instantaneous potential energy −αE2/2. Averaging over one optical cycle gives
Ugrad​=−41​α∣E0​∣2,Fgrad​=−∇Ugrad​=2nm​ϵ0​cα​∇I.

Thus np​>nm​ gives positive polarizability and attraction toward larger light intensity; np​<nm​ reverses this contribution. The factor 1/4 uses a peak field: substituting a root mean square field without changing that factor would halve the force incorrectly. Dimensionally α∣E0​∣2 is energy, so its gradient is force.
This leading conservative term does not remove the optical scattering force. Even a nonabsorbing induced electric dipole reradiates light: at fixed wavelength and index contrast, its Rayleigh scattering cross-section scales as a6, while α scales as a3. A smaller bead can therefore improve the ratio of gradient to scattering forces while weakening the well relative to kB​T, where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant and T the temperature. Optical force balance and resistance to thermal escape are separate questions. Intermediate bead sizes require a wave-scattering calculation; neither a ray calculation nor this small-dipole expression is uniformly valid there.

Optical tweezers OurBigBook.com
An optical scattering force transfers momentum from light to a particle through scattering of light. In a usual single-beam optical trap, its axial contribution pushes along beam propagation; the optical gradient force must balance it for axial confinement. This balance can place the stable equilibrium away from the beam focus.

Three-dimensional optical trap stability (Fi​≃−ki​δri​,ki​>0)

Words: 194
Optical tweezers OurBigBook.com
At an equilibrium r∗​, the total force vanishes. A small transverse displacement must produce a transverse restoring force; a small axial displacement must also restore the bead. Downstream of a tight focus, the backward optical gradient force can oppose the forward optical scattering force. Equality at one point is insufficient: the total axial force must decrease as the bead moves downstream through that point. The equilibrium can therefore lie downstream of the intensity maximum.
For uncoupled overdamped coordinates, ζi​δri​˙​=−ki​δri​ with ζi​>0 decays only when each ki​>0. More generally, linearizing gives δr˙=MJδr, where M is the hydrodynamic mobility matrix and Jij​=∂Fi​/∂rj​ at equilibrium. All eigenvalues of MJ must have negative real parts for linear asymptotic stability. For a conservative force with symmetric positive-definite mobility, a positive-definite Hessian matrix of the potential energy supplies this condition. A general optical force need not possess a global potential energy.
Increasing numerical aperture admits more strongly converging light rays and a steeper axial variation of the field. But a larger nominal numerical aperture alone does not establish trapping: illumination of the objective pupil, optical aberration, particle properties and the actual in-liquid focus also matter. A harmonic optical trap describes local confinement after this stability question has been answered; it does not predict capture from arbitrary positions or an infinite holding force.

A harmonic optical trap approximates one coordinate near a stable equilibrium by a quadratic potential energy. Measure displacement x from that equilibrium, set its potential energy to zero there, and take a positive effective spring constant k, also called the trap stiffness:
U(x)=21​kx2,F(x)=−dxdU​=−kx,k>0.
(25)
The restoring force points left when x>0 and right when x<0. This is a local model: a Taylor series of a smooth potential energy about a nondegenerate local minimum gives k=U′′(0)>0 as its leading curvature. A real optical trap has a finite capture region; the endlessly rising parabola does not describe its escape boundary. A three-dimensional optical trap can have different stiffnesses along different axes, and nonconservative optical forces can limit the potential energy description.

Repeat the calibration after changing trapping power or optics.
