Coronagraph

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Optics OurBigBook.com
A coronagraph is an optical instrument that suppresses a bright source's light before detection while transmitting some light from nearby directions. Its purpose is to reveal faint structure buried in the bright source's point spread function, as in exoplanet direct imaging. A Lyot coronagraph combines a coronagraphic focal plane mask with a Lyot stop in a reimaged optical pupil; blocking the central image alone does not remove its diffraction rings. [ref].
The original motivation was the solar corona: hiding the bright photosphere would allow longer, repeated observations of faint surrounding light. In his 1930 paper, Lyot explained that short total eclipses restricted observing time and prevented some long exposures for spectral lines. The attraction is an instrument that makes the faint neighborhood accessible on demand. [ref]. The Sun is an extended source; the point-source calculation below illustrates imaging of an unresolved star and is not a quantitative model of the solar corona.

Lyot coronagraph

Words: 944 Articles: 4
Coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A classical Lyot coronagraph first forms an image of a bright source on the optical axis. A coronagraphic focal plane mask hides its core. Relay optics then form an image of the entrance pupil, where a Lyot stop blocks the outer rim and, when needed, borders around internal obstructions. Finally an optical camera forms the science image. The focal plane sorts incoming directions into image positions; the optical pupil sorts contributions across the aperture. This change of plane makes it possible to reject additional stellar light that survives the first mask. [ref].

Coronagraphic focal plane mask

Words: 59
Lyot coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A coronagraphic focal plane mask modifies the wave amplitude or wave phase in an intermediate focal plane. Here it is a perfectly opaque circular disk centered on the bright source. A finite aperture produces an extended point spread function, so a finite disk blocks only part of the stellar light. Its sharp edge also changes the transmitted field and hence the later diffraction pattern. The exact model below makes both effects visible.

Lyot stop

Words: 65
Lyot coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A Lyot stop is a mask in the reimaged optical pupil after a coronagraphic focal plane mask. For an unobstructed circular entrance pupil, it usually transmits a smaller concentric disk. In a classical Lyot coronagraph, much of the residual stellar field lies near the optical pupil boundary; the Lyot stop rejects that field before the final image is formed. It also rejects useful off-axis light, so choosing its opening involves a coronagraph throughput tradeoff. [ref].

(36)

Outside the disk M=1, so the local wave intensity is still ∣A∣2: hiding the core has left those rings intact. Reimaging an unlimited pupil gives
EL​=F−1(MA)=P−P∗F−1W,Afinal​=F(LEL​),Ifinal​=∣Afinal​∣2,
(37)
where ∗ is convolution, L is the Lyot stop transmission, and the proportionality constant in the irradiance is omitted. Coordinate reversals from physical relay optics are absorbed into the coordinate choice. These equations use wave amplitudes throughout propagation; applying a Fourier transform to wave intensity would give a different and incorrect model. This is the pupil/image calculation described by Sivaramakrishnan et al.; the circular disk and numerical choices below are our illustrative specialization. [ref].
The subtraction explains the beauty of the arrangement: in much of the interior, the original pupil field and the convolution term nearly cancel. Near a boundary, that cancellation is incomplete. The Lyot stop can therefore block a region containing disproportionately much unwanted light. A hard-edged coronagraphic focal plane mask has a transform with extended tails, so the interior need not be perfectly dark. With an unlimited relay, L=1 gives Afinal​=MA exactly: no further ring suppression occurs. A stop covering the full original optical pupil instead uses L=P and already clips field outside the optical pupil; an undersized Lyot stop clips more of the remaining rim.
The toy uses a coronagraphic focal plane mask of angular radius 3λ/D and a Lyot stop of diameter 0.8D. The discrete Fourier transform grid has 1024×1024 samples, with 128 across D and angular sampling 0.125λ/D; it approximates the continuous equations on a finite periodic domain. The plot averages wave intensity in annuli of width 0.25λ/D. Over the annulus 4≤∣u∣≤10, the mean wave intensity divided by the direct stellar peak is approximately 1.40×10−4 without a coronagraph, the same with only the focal mask and an unlimited relay, 4.44×10−5 with the mask and full pupil, and 1.66×10−6 with the mask and 0.8D Lyot stop. Thus the undersized opening reduces this particular annular mean about 27-fold relative to the full-pupil comparison. It does not suppress every direction by that factor, and these values do not predict a real instrument's detection limit.
The ideal toy excludes a central obstruction, support vanes, scattering of light, wavefront errors, atmospheric effects, a spread of wavelengths, pointing drift and detector noise. It also contains only the star: no simulated planet or solar corona. For a far off-axis source whose image misses the coronagraphic focal plane mask, the continuous geometric coronagraph throughput of the 0.8D opening tends to 0.82=0.64 relative to the full disk. Rejecting stellar light therefore costs some desired light as well. Enlarging the coronagraphic focal plane mask narrows the characteristic scale of its pupil-plane transform by the scaling property of the Fourier transform, but also hides a larger neighborhood of the source.

Raman scattering

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Scattering of light OurBigBook.com
Raman scattering is inelastic scattering of light in which the outgoing photon has a different frequency because matter gains or loses internal energy. Molecular vibration is a particularly useful recipient: a visible photon can reveal an internal energy spacing normally associated with infrared frequencies. Rayleigh scattering supplies the much stronger, approximately unchanged-frequency reference. The distinction concerns the transferred energy, rather than merely a change of direction or the colour of the illuminating beam.
The elementary bookkeeping is conservation of energy:
hν0​+Ei​=hνs​+Ef​,h(ν0​−νs​)=Ef​−Ei​.
(38)
Here h is the Planck constant, ν0​ and νs​ are the incident and scattered photon frequencies, and Ei​,Ef​ are initial and final internal molecular energies. This expression neglects translational recoil and Doppler broadening; those can matter in sufficiently precise gas measurements. A positive internal energy change gives Stokes Raman scattering, and a negative one gives Anti-Stokes Raman scattering. The energy difference determines a possible line position, but it does not by itself establish that a transition is optically allowed or predict its strength.
The spontaneous molecular process developed here has a connection to the Raman transition used in atomic measurement methods: two photon interactions transfer an internal energy difference. Coherently driving that process with two applied light fields is a different experimental regime from collecting weak spontaneous Raman scattering beside an illuminating beam.

Raman and Krishnan light-scattering experiment

Words: 489
Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman and Kariamanikkam Srinivasa Krishnan jointly reported the effect in 1928. Their letter describes light from the Sun concentrated by an 18cm-aperture, 230cm-focal length telescope objective and a second optical lens onto a liquid purified by repeated vacuum distillation. With blue-violet and yellow-green optical filters together in the incident beam, the visible track disappeared; moving the yellow-green optical filter between liquid and observer restored it. The complementary arrangement rejected unchanged-colour scattering of light while admitting newly generated light. Persistence after purification and strong wave polarization in many liquids argued against ordinary fluorescent contamination.[ref]
In his 1930 lecture, Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman describes a cobalt-glass optical filter selecting indigo-violet light from the Sun, with a separated blue-green band in the scattered optical spectrum. Substituting a quartz mercury arc and condenser gave sharp new spectral lines. Small Hilger quartz spectrographs recorded them photographically; Kariamanikkam Srinivasa Krishnan obtained more precise records with a larger instrument and established violet-displaced lines. The optical prism disperses wavelengths for spatial readout; it does not create the Raman shift. The diagram gives functional optical paths rather than a reconstruction of a specific Hilger instrument.[ref]
Their May 1928 report strengthens the comparison: filtered mercury illumination of toluene produced extra spectral lines. Removing the 4358A˚ incident line removed its associated longer-wavelength group; a quinine filter removing the 4047, 4078 and 4109A˚ group removed a different shifted group while preserving the one associated with 4358A˚. These are actual selective-excitation controls, rather than inferred colours.[ref]
The inference has limits. A complementary-filter test alone establishes newly admitted wavelengths, not their precise spacing or a unique microscopic mechanism. Fluorescence can also survive purification when intrinsic to the liquid, and fluorescence can be polarized. Useful distinctions therefore combine resolved spectral lines, excitation dependence, wave polarization and sample preparation. A proposed modern extension is to change a single incident frequency: a molecular Raman shift should follow the same internal energy gap, whereas ordinary relaxed molecular fluorescence usually retains approximately its emission-band positions. This is a diagnostic under stated conditions, not a universal theorem about every fluorescent material or resonant scattering process. Raman scattering need not involve a populated, relaxed electronic excited state as ordinary molecular fluorescence does; neither a redder photon nor the word Stokes identifies the mechanism by itself.
The 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman alone for his work on scattering of light and the discovery of the effect. That award allocation should be distinguished from the joint experimental report with Kariamanikkam Srinivasa Krishnan.[ref]

Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
The signed Raman shift subtracts scattered from incident spectroscopic wavenumber:
Δν=cν0​−νs​​=λ0​1​−λs​1​=hcEf​−Ei​​.
(39)
Here c is the speed of light, and both wavelengths are in vacuum. Positive shifts denote Stokes Raman scattering; negative shifts denote Anti-Stokes Raman scattering. Some plots reverse the horizontal direction or report separate unsigned magnitudes, so check the convention. Spectroscopic wavenumber has no 2π factor, unlike the common angular wavenumber k=2π/λ. A shift of 1000cm−1 means 100000m−1, not a frequency of 1000Hz.
For a one-quantum change of molecular vibration with ordinary frequency νv​, the magnitude is νv​=νv​/c. This makes Raman spectroscopy attractive: the same molecular energy spacing can be read using different visible excitation wavelengths. Equal and opposite Raman shifts are not equal and opposite changes measured in nanometres, because wavelength is the reciprocal of spectroscopic wavenumber.

Stokes Raman scattering (νs​=ν0​−νv​)

Words: 57
Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
In Stokes Raman scattering, matter gains internal energy and the photon loses the same amount. For a quantum harmonic oscillator representing one molecular vibration, Ev​=hνv​(v+1/2) with v=0,1,…. The transition v→v+1 gives νs​=ν0​−νv​, requiring ν0​>νv​ for an outgoing photon. Even a molecule initially in its vibrational ground state can undergo this process. The shared name does not turn it into the absorption/emission-band Stokes shift used for fluorescence.

Anti-Stokes Raman scattering (νs​=ν0​+νv​)

Words: 54
Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
In Anti-Stokes Raman scattering, matter loses internal energy and the outgoing photon gains it. The harmonic transition v→v−1 requires v≥1, so an initially excited vibrational population must be available. At low temperature, high-frequency vibrational excitations are scarce and the corresponding anti-Stokes line is weak. The extra photon energy comes from the molecule; there is no conflict with conservation of energy.

Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
The simplest off-resonant explanation is a vibrating polarizability. Let Q(t)=Q0​cos(2πνv​t) be a small normal mode coordinate of molecular vibration, and use one scalar component of polarizability, α(Q)≃α0​+α0′​Q. For incident electric field E(t)=E0​cos(2πν0​t), the induced electric dipole moment is
p(t)​=α(Q(t))E(t)=α0​E0​cos(2πν0​t)+2α0′​Q0​E0​​[cos(2π(ν0​−νv​)t)+cos(2π(ν0​+νv​)t)].​
(40)
The product-to-sum formula produces the two displaced frequencies. A nonzero derivative α0′​ gives vibrational Raman scattering in this linear model. Real polarizability is generally a tensor, and the selected components depend on incident and observed wave polarization. This condition differs from vibrational infrared activity, which requires a changing molecular electric dipole moment without an applied optical electric field. A vibration can therefore appear in one measurement and be absent in the other.
This classical modulation argument explains line locations but supplies equal sideband wave amplitudes; it does not explain their thermal asymmetry or the nonzero Stokes Raman scattering from a vibrational ground state. Those require the quantum harmonic oscillator population and transition strengths. The far-off-resonance drawing uses dashed virtual intermediate levels: they represent terms in a scattering probability amplitude, not a long-lived occupied electronic energy eigenstate. Near an electronic resonance, a more detailed treatment of the intermediate response is needed.

Thermal Raman line ratio (IAS​/IS​)

Raman scattering OurBigBook.com
Assume one harmonic normal mode at thermal equilibrium, weak spontaneous excitation far from electronic resonances, the same collection solid angle and wave polarization, and matched response after instrumental correction. The Boltzmann distribution gives
r=exp(−kB​Thνv​​),Pv​=(1−r)rv,v=1−rr​.
(41)
Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, T>0 is temperature, and Pv​ is the probability of vibrational quantum number v. Thus P1​/P0​=r. Linear coupling to Q has squared oscillator matrix elements proportional to v+1 for Stokes Raman scattering and v for Anti-Stokes Raman scattering. Summing over initial levels gives strengths proportional to v+1 and v respectively; their ratio is r, even when levels above v=1 are occupied.
Let IS​ and IAS​ denote line-integrated radiant intensities, meaning power per collection solid angle. The off-resonant electric dipole radiation law adds the fourth power of emitted frequency:
IS​IAS​​=(ν0​−νv​ν0​+νv​​)4exp(−kB​Thνv​​).
(42)
The photon rate divides each line's power by its own hνs​. Consequently, the ideal response-corrected anti-Stokes/Stokes count-rate ratio has the third power of the same frequency ratio. Peak heights alone do not give line-integrated radiant intensities if linewidths differ. Uncorrected detector counts can also include unequal detector response and unequal optical filter transmission. Resonant enhancement, overlapping spectral lines, nonthermal populations and local optical heating can invalidate a temperature inferred from this simple formula.

Raman spectroscopy

Words: 254 Articles: 3
Raman scattering OurBigBook.com Tags: Spectroscopy
Raman spectroscopy measures shifted scattering of light to infer internal energy spacings and the molecular response that makes them visible. In a modern illustrative arrangement, narrowband laser illumination replaces the historical arc, an optical filter rejects the strong excitation line, and a spectrograph resolves the weak shifted spectral lines. The illumination, rejection and spectral dispersion are separate jobs. Increasing rejection can conceal small Raman shifts close to the excitation line.
A proposed measurement should record the excitation wavelength, a dark signal, a blank container and the liquid, then compare calibrated line positions and integrated signals under the same collection conditions. Measure optical filter transmission and detector response before using the Thermal Raman line ratio for temperature. Repeat at lower incident power to look for heating or altered sample response. These are suggested checks, not an assertion that the 1928 apparatus implemented modern calibration procedures.
Its appeal is the conversion of internal molecular energy differences into visible spectral lines: changing the excitation can move the whole pattern while preserving characteristic Raman shifts. Combined with vibrational infrared activity, Raman vibrational activity supplies complementary information about molecular vibration. A line pattern can constrain a material's identity or environment, but overlapping bands, fluorescence backgrounds and the finite spectral resolution element prevent an unqualified identification from one peak alone.

Aperture

Words: 595 Articles: 3
Optics OurBigBook.com
An aperture is an opening that admits light into or through an optical instrument. Its shape and size select the transmitted light rays; an aperture alone does not bend them as an optical lens does. The aperture stop is the opening that most restricts the bundle from an on-axis object point. The entrance pupil is the image of that aperture stop formed by the preceding optical lens elements, viewed from the object side. Consequently the effective collecting diameter D is the entrance pupil diameter, which can differ from the physical hole's diameter. For example, preceding optical lens elements that enlarge a 10mm aperture stop by a factor of two give D=20mm; measuring the physical hole alone would misidentify the focal ratio. [ref].
For an unobscured circular entrance pupil under a uniform beam normal to its plane, the collecting area and admitted radiant flux are
A=4πD2​,Φadmitted​=Epupil​A,
(44)
where Epupil​ is incident irradiance. Doubling D quadruples admitted radiant flux. Obstructions, nonuniform illumination and losses after the entrance pupil require the actual illuminated area and transmission to be included. The same D also sets an angular diffraction-limited resolution scale λ/D at wavelength λ. Collection and diffraction therefore answer different questions from field of view: an aperture selects the bundle from each object point, while the receiving plane's extent helps select which object directions appear in the image.
NASA/JPL's published pinhole demonstration uses two white cards, foil taped over a window in one card, and a small hole pierced in the foil. Sunlight passes through the hole onto the second card; the projected image is viewed on that card. The activity describes a larger image when the card separation increases, improved visibility when the receiving card is shaded, and a separate image from each of several holes. These are qualitative observations of image formation, rather than calibrated measurements of radiant flux or diffraction. [ref].
A proposed quantitative extension replaces sunlight by a steadily illuminated asymmetric target and puts the foil and a translucent receiving screen in a dark box. Record target distance u, hole-to-screen distance b, hole diameter d, image height, orientation and edge blur. Measure screen brightness with a fixed photodetector, or record the screen with an optical camera whose integration time and gain stay fixed. Exchange centred foils of measured d at fixed u,b; then vary b with the same foil. Geometrical optics predicts an inverted image with transverse magnification m=−b/u and a point's geometric blur diameter d(1+b/u). Thus a larger hole admits more radiant flux without changing the central image scale, whereas increasing b enlarges the image. These are predictions to test, not reported data. Keep target illumination and detector position fixed, subtract a hole-covered dark reading, repeat the original foil to check drift, and avoid clipping the detector response. Foil thickness and ragged edges can block oblique light rays; at sufficiently small d, diffraction invalidates the claim that ever smaller holes always sharpen the image. A lensless optical camera has no optical lens focal length: b is a propagation distance, not that focal length.

Infrared

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Optics OurBigBook.com
Infrared is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than the red end of ordinarily visible light. A useful named convention is the CIE range 780nm to 1mm; the approximate visible range 400–700nm used in some teaching texts puts the boundary nearer 700nm. [ref]. Neither number is a sharp physical cutoff of human vision. The CIE divisions IR-A, IR-B and IR-C are respectively 0.78–1.4μm, 1.4–3μm and 3–1000μm; the boundaries of near-, middle- and far-infrared vary between applications. [ref].
Use vacuum wavelength λ when comparing these ranges. With frequency ν, speed of light c, Planck constant h and photon energy E,
ν=λc​,E=hν=λhc​.
(45)
Thus the CIE infrared interval corresponds approximately to 3.00×1011–3.84×1014Hz and 1.99×10−22–2.55×10−19J per photon, with the smaller energy at the longer wavelength. A 940nm infrared photon has E≃2.11×10−19J, whereas a 254nm ultraviolet photon has E≃7.82×10−19J. These are calculations from hc/λ, not measurements of a particular source. A television remote is a familiar approximately 940nm source; its information is carried by variations in the emitted radiant flux. [ref].
Detection and visual perception answer different questions. A photodetector can respond to infrared even when an observer perceives no light; a thermometer detects an increase in temperature after photon absorption. Conversely, a small readout can reflect a small spectral responsivity, rather than absence of incident electromagnetic radiation. Images made from infrared readouts use display colors chosen by the imaging system; those colors are not the colors of the incoming infrared.
The important microscopic mechanisms also differ. In infrared spectroscopy, photon absorption often increases the energy of a normal mode in which chemical bonds stretch or bend. The corresponding optical spectrum helps distinguish molecules by their motions. For the usual electric dipole mechanism, the motion must change the electric dipole moment; matching the frequency alone is not sufficient. [ref]. Electronic processes can also emit or absorb infrared, so it is not exclusively radiation from molecular motion. [ref]; [ref].
Infrared is especially useful for observing thermal radiation from objects near everyday temperatures. For an ideal 300K blackbody, Wien's displacement law gives a wavelength peak near 9.66μm. A thermal camera's readout nevertheless depends on emissivity, reflected surroundings and transmission along the path, as well as temperature. [ref]. A source emitting infrared need not be hot: an infrared remote is useful precisely because a photodetector can distinguish its signal from a background. Visible light and ultraviolet can also cause heating when absorbed; “infrared” names a wavelength range, not a unique form of heat.
Herschel's 1800 discovery made the distinction between sight and detection experimentally concrete. His report describes a optical prism spreading sunlight across a white, ruled receiving surface, with three thermometers at different positions near the end of the visible optical spectrum. He observed heating beyond the red edge where no visible color appeared. The result established that sunlight contained invisible radiation less strongly refracted by that optical prism than the visible red; it did not measure a photon energy or establish today's infrared boundaries. [ref]; [ref].
A documented modern version by Caltech/IPAC uses a glass optical prism, white paper in a shaded box and three blackened liquid-filled thermometers. Initial readings in shade provide each thermometer's baseline; subsequent readings compare blue, yellow and just beyond red after the bulbs have had time to warm. The measured quantity is the rise in temperature, not a “temperature of a color”. The lesson reports the expected largest rise beyond visible red and specifically discusses matching the bulb coatings and thermometer calibration. Clouds and changes in the projected optical spectrum affect the comparison. [ref].
For a stronger modern interpretation, an additional shaded thermometer would monitor ambient drift, exchanging bulbs between positions would test differences between thermometers, and blocking the incident beam would distinguish beam-dependent heating from warmed supports or air. These are suggested controls, not claims about Herschel's historical procedure. Thermal conduction through the mounting and convection can change the readout. A broad bulb also samples a range of wavelengths; the optical prism's transmission and optical dispersion, the bulb's absorption and heat loss all affect the position of the largest rise. In particular, the result does not show that an infrared photon carries more energy than a visible photon.
A simple analytical illustration makes those limitations explicit. Let θ=T−Tamb​ be the bulb's excess temperature, C its heat capacity, G its effective heat-loss coefficient in WK−1, and Pabs​ the absorbed power. Assume one uniform bulb temperature, constant ambient temperature, constant C,G, and losses linear in θ. Then
Cdtdθ​=Pabs​−Gθ,θ(t)=GPabs​​(1−e−t/τ),τ=GC​,
(46)
for a beam switched on at t=0 with θ(0)=0. After switching the beam off at t=ts​, θ(t)=θ(ts​)e−(t−ts​)/τ. The exponential function follows by solving this linear differential equation. The steady excess temperature measures Pabs​/G; it is not a direct measurement of the optical spectrum. With illustrative C=0.020JK−1 and G=0.0010WK−1, τ=20s. Absorbed powers of 1.0 and 0.5mW give steady rises of 1.0 and 0.5K, regardless of which wavelengths supplied that absorbed power.
The upper schematic represents the logic of the optical prism experiment; its light ray positions are not a calibrated wavelength scale. The lower curves use the illustrative heat-balance model, with the beam blocked at 60s; they are not historical or modern measured data. The beauty of the experiment is that a simple change of detector extends observation beyond what the eye can perceive.

Ultraviolet

Words: 925 Articles: 1
Optics OurBigBook.com
Ultraviolet is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than the violet end of ordinarily visible light. The CIE convention uses 100–400nm, subdivided into UV-A at 315–400nm, UV-B at 280–315nm and UV-C at 100–280nm. These divisions name intervals; they do not mark universal changes in every material's response. The boundary with visible light is not sharp, and other fields use near-, far-, vacuum- and extreme-ultraviolet divisions. [ref]. For example, NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory observes extreme-ultraviolet bands below 100nm; the CIE interval is therefore not the full extent of astronomical ultraviolet usage. [ref].
The CIE ultraviolet interval corresponds to frequencies about 7.49×1014–3.00×1015Hz and photon energies 4.97×10−19–1.99×10−18J, using vacuum wavelength and E=hc/λ with Planck constant h and speed of light c. Shorter wavelength means larger energy per photon; larger irradiance means more incident power per area. These are different comparisons. At the same incident power, a 254nm ultraviolet beam has fewer photons per second than a 940nm infrared beam, even though each ultraviolet photon has more energy.
A common ultraviolet mechanism is photon absorption promoting an electron from a ground state to an excited state of a chemical atom or molecule. By contrast, many infrared absorption bands involve stretching or bending chemical bonds. For either mechanism, both the energy difference and the coupling to the incident electromagnetic field matter. One concrete example is the 217nm absorption discussed for butadiene: an electron moves between molecular orbitals, and the position of the absorption reveals their energy separation. Ultraviolet absorption can therefore probe molecular orbitals, while infrared spectroscopy probes many molecular motions. [ref].
Subsequent chemical reactions depend on the absorbing chemical substance and its environment; the label ultraviolet alone does not predict a reaction rate. At sufficiently short wavelength, a photon can cause photoionization if its energy exceeds the relevant ionization energy. There is no single wavelength that separates all ionizing from all nonionizing behavior for every chemical substance. Likewise, eventual heating after photon absorption is possible in both ultraviolet and infrared. The distinction is useful because different optical spectra expose different processes, not because the two ranges obey different laws of electromagnetism.
Ritter's 1801 observation used a chemical readout rather than a thermometer. In Caltech/IPAC's account, sunlight passed through a glass optical prism and silver chloride was placed in different parts of the optical spectrum. Darkening was weak toward red, stronger toward violet, and pronounced beyond the visible violet edge. The measured evidence was a change in the chemical substance's appearance at a spatial location with no visible color, establishing radiation beyond the eye's ordinary range. It was not a calibrated measurement of a universal ultraviolet optical spectrum. [ref].
A controlled modern interpretation of such a chemical test would compare equal exposure durations and matched fresh samples, keep an unexposed sample in darkness, monitor temperature, and distinguish scattered visible light from the intended short-wavelength beam with characterized filtering. These are proposed controls, not an assertion that Ritter performed them. Unequal sample preparation or heating can change a reaction rate. The optical prism, terrestrial atmosphere and sample response restrict which wavelengths the test detects. Darkening is a detector-weighted response, so its spatial maximum is not automatically the maximum of incoming radiant flux or of photon energy.
Thomas Larason and Jeanne Houston's NIST report documents a quantitative ultraviolet detector comparison. An argon source feeds a double-diffraction grating spectrometer; a shutter and mirrors deliver the selected band to a working-standard or test photodiode, successively at the same position. A beam splitter supplies a monitor photodiode. Amplifiers and voltmeters record detector and monitor simultaneously; shutter-closed readings provide dark baselines. The 200–500nm scan, typically with 4nm bandpass, measures spectral responsivity. Monitor normalization suppresses source drift; known spectral lines calibrate wavelength. The report assesses temperature effects and unwanted light outside the band, weighted by detector response. The latter need not cancel between different spectral responsivities. [ref].
This determines electrical response without visual perception. Bandpass and spatial nonuniformity limit the calibration; aging and changed temperature can affect later use. The scan includes visible light and ultraviolet; no response below 200nm follows from it.
For a narrow beam, the idealized substitution calculation is
Rtest​(λ)=Rstd​(λ)Istd​/Mstd​Itest​/Mtest​​.
(47)
Here R is spectral responsivity; I and M are dark-subtracted detector and monitor electric currents. This follows by writing I=RP for each detector and using the monitor to track changes in radiant flux. It assumes linear response, unchanged beam splitting and collection geometry, and a sufficiently narrow band. For an illustrative standard with Rstd​=0.15AW−1, ratios Istd​/Mstd​=2.0 and Itest​/Mtest​=1.6 give Rtest​=0.12AW−1. These invented arithmetic inputs illustrate the method; they are not NIST measurements.
An independent photon-counting model connects spectral responsivity to quantum efficiency. If η(λ) is the number of collected electrons per incident photon, there is no internal multiplication, and q is the elementary charge, then
N˙=hcPλ​,I=qηN˙,R(λ)=PI​=η(λ)hcqλ​.
(48)
At illustrative constant η=0.60 and P=1μW, this gives about 0.123μA at 254nm and 0.455μA at 940nm. The ultraviolet readout is smaller in this model because there are fewer incident photons, not because their individual energies are smaller. Real quantum efficiency depends on wavelength, windows, absorption and carrier collection; a detector's band gap and construction determine its usable range. Constant η across these two wavelengths is an analytical comparison, not a claimed specification of a real photodiode.
The curve is the calculated relation E=hc/λ, and the shaded ranges use the stated CIE conventions. The lower diagram abstracts the detector comparison rather than reproducing an instrument drawing. Together with the infrared heat-balance illustration, it shows why a calibrated detector response, rather than what looks bright to an observer, is the bridge between invisible radiation and a quantitative measurement.

Astronomical seeing is the atmospheric blurring of a stellar image, conventionally expressed as the angular full width at half maximum of its long-exposure point spread function, usually in arcseconds. For a large aperture in the ideal Kolmogorov model, it is approximately 0.98λ/r0​ radians, with Fried parameter r0​.

Calibrated Fourier statistics of short-exposure speckle patterns recover information suppressed by a long seeing-blurred exposure. The exposure must adequately freeze turbulence and the source must supply enough photons; noise and calibrator mismatch limit the reconstruction.

Many short frames freeze atmospheric image fluctuations. Selecting the sharpest frames, registering them and combining them can improve angular resolution. Selection discards photons and can create a read-noise penalty, so adequate reference-source photon counts are essential. It does not guarantee that every high-order wavefront error disappears.

Lippmann plate

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Optics OurBigBook.com
A Lippmann plate records colour as a depth-dependent optical structure in a photographic emulsion. A standing wave writes a spacing; wave interference during later illumination selects the reflected wavelengths. This makes a photographic plate a spatial record of an optical spectrum. The striking idea is that information about colour can live in geometry.
Gabriel Lippmann presented his colour process in 1891 and received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physics. His career belongs principally to physics: he held chairs in mathematical and experimental physics.[ref] [ref]

Lippmann colour-recording experiment

Words: 246
Lippmann plate OurBigBook.com
In his 14 December 1908 Nobel lecture, Gabriel Lippmann described a photographic plate bearing a transparent, even, extremely fine sensitive layer. A holder put Mercury against that layer as a mirror during exposure. Incident and reflected light formed a standing wave within the photographic emulsion; after photographic processing and drying, white light revealed colour by selective reflection. The reflector served during recording; the developed structure supplied the later colour selection.[ref]
The lecture's control was to project a spectrum photograph, wet it, and project it again. Its colours disappeared as the gelatin swelled, then returned during drying, red before the shorter wavelengths. This tested a spacing-dependent explanation. Lippmann also reported roughly one-minute sunlight exposures and identified portrait exposure time as a limitation.[ref]
A reversible colour change supports a structural explanation, but does not independently measure every fringe spacing or the refractive index. For a conceptual comparison, record a narrow band and compare reflected optical spectra at fixed illumination and viewing angles; an unexposed processed plate tests background. A second comparison changes only viewing geometry. A third compares the dry state before and after a reversible spacing change. These are proposed discriminating controls, not additional experiments attributed to Lippmann. Background surface reflection must be separated from the selective signal. A photograph's appearance also depends on the illuminating optical spectrum; viewing under an arbitrary lamp is not a calibrated spectral measurement.

Lippmann fringe spacing (d=λ0​/(2n))

Words: 325
Lippmann plate OurBigBook.com
At normal incidence, let z measure distance from the reflector into a uniform transparent layer with refractive index n. For a monochromatic wave of vacuum wavelength λ0​, the layer wavenumber is k=2πn/λ0​. Represent the incident and returning electric fields by complex wave amplitudes with time factor e−iωt suppressed:
Ei​(z)=E0​e−ikz,Er​(z)=rE0​eikz,r=∣r∣eiϕ.
(49)
The time-averaged squared electric field, normalized to the incident contribution, is
⟨Ei2​⟩⟨E2⟩​=1+∣r∣2+2∣r∣cos(2kz+ϕ).
(50)
This electric exposure pattern has maxima separated by
2kd=2π,d=kπ​=2nλ0​​.
(51)
The wave phase of the reflector shifts the maxima's positions but leaves their spacing unchanged in this uniform-layer model. The electric pattern, rather than the zero net energy flux of an ideal standing wave, is the relevant exposure proxy. An imperfect mirror reduces its contrast: (Imax​−Imin​)/(Imax​+Imin​)=2∣r∣/(1+∣r∣2), where I denotes this exposure proxy.
Choose λ0​=600nm and n=1.5. Then the medium wavelength is 400nm and d=200nm. For an ideal phase-reversing reflector, r=−1 and the normalized pattern is 4sin2(kz): its first two maxima are at z=100 and 300nm. These are chosen calculations, not measured properties of a historical photographic emulsion or the optical response of Mercury.
For multiple mutually incoherent wavelengths, time averaging adds exposure contributions rather than their instantaneous electric fields. In a linearized recording model,
D(z)∝∫S(λ0​)q(λ0​)[1+∣r(λ0​)∣2+2∣r(λ0​)∣cos(λ0​4πn(λ0​)z​+ϕ(λ0​))]dλ0​.
(52)
Here S is incident spectral exposure density, q a wavelength-dependent recording sensitivity and D a model exposure response. An optical spectrum therefore writes overlapping depth oscillations, not necessarily visibly separated sheets. This is a useful connection to the Fourier transform: approximately, depth is paired with optical spatial frequency 2n/λ0​. Finite recording depth, varying sensitivity and nonlinear photographic processing prevent treating this expression as an exact inversion rule for an actual plate.

Finite-layer model of Lippmann reflection (λB​=2ndcosθ)

Words: 485
Lippmann plate OurBigBook.com
To isolate the readout mechanism, replace the processed photographic emulsion by N equally spaced, identical weak scattering planes, with separation d. Take the readout refractive index n to be real and independent of wavelength, and let θ be the internal angle from the plane normal. Adjacent specularly backscattered contributions differ in wave phase by 2kz​d=4πndcosθ/λ0​. Their geometric series gives
rN​=a∑j=0N−1​eijδ,δ=λ0​4πndcosθ​−2π,FN​=N2∣a∣2∣rN​∣2​=[Nsin(δ/2)sin(Nδ/2)​]2.
(53)
Here a is a small plane reflection wave amplitude, assumed constant in this illustrative band; FN​=1 at δ=0 by continuity. Since incident and reflected waves occupy the same external medium, ∣rN​∣2 is the model reflectance when transmission factors are absorbed into a. Require N∣a∣≪1 for the weak-scattering sum to remain self-consistent. Normalizing to FN​ discards absolute brightness; it does not predict a highly reflecting historical plate.
The first-order peak obeys
λB​=2ndcosθ.
(54)
This is Bragg's law with an angle measured from the normal, rather than the glancing Bragg angle. For external viewing angle α in air approximated by refractive index one, Snell's law gives nsinθ=sinα, hence
λB​(α)=2nd1−n2sin2α​​.
(55)
The expression describes specular readout: illumination must supply the matching incident direction. Tilting a plate under fixed narrow illumination can make the signal disappear as well as change its selected colour.
For the chosen n=1.5 and d=200nm, calculated peaks are 600nm at α=0, 565.69nm at 30∘, and 529.15nm at 45∘. Greater obliquity selects a shorter wavelength. Uniform shrinkage to d′=sd, with unchanged n, multiplies every peak wavelength by s: a chosen s=0.95 moves the normal peak to 570nm. More generally, λB′​/λB​=(n′/n)s at normal incidence. A change of thickness alone is insufficient if processing also changes the refractive index.
Finite N gives a finite spectral response. The nearest zeros satisfy δ=±2π/N, giving λ±​=λB​/(1±1/N). At the normal 600nm peak, N=30 gives neighbouring zeros at approximately 580.65 and 620.69nm; N=10 gives 545.45 and 666.67nm. Thus greater sampled depth narrows the central band in this model. The small-detuning distance from peak to a nearest zero is approximately λB​/N; it is not the full width at half maximum.
Real processed photographic emulsions have a continuous, irregular depth response rather than identical planes. Absorption, wavelength-dependent refractive index, unequal scattering strengths, a nonideal exposure reflector, changes during photographic processing and multiple scattering of light can alter both peak positions and shapes. A transfer calculation with measured material parameters would be needed for quantitative reflectance. The present model explains the phase-selection mechanism and the tradeoff between depth and spectral width; it cannot establish faithful reproduction of an arbitrary incident optical spectrum. Its useful lesson is that a photograph can record colour through sub-wavelength structure, while its eventual appearance still depends on illumination, viewing geometry and processing.

Nonlinear optics

Words: 3k Articles: 53
Optics OurBigBook.com
Nonlinear optics studies the response of matter to light when the induced electric polarization is not proportional to the driving electric field. An intense laser can make these additional terms observable. The striking consequence is that a material can emit light at a frequency absent from the incident beam: second-harmonic generation doubles it. This extends a laser's usable optical spectrum without requiring a second lasing transition.
Franken and colleagues frequency-doubling experiment established an optical harmonic in 1961. Nicolaas Bloembergen's theoretical work developed the description of interacting light waves in nonlinear matter. His 1981 lecture connects a nonlinear constitutive relation with Maxwell's equations and explains compensation of optical dispersion by birefringence.[ref]

A crystal used for its nonlinear optics response, allowing processes such as spontaneous parametric down-conversion when the appropriate phase matching is satisfied.

Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
Nonlinear polarization is the part of an induced electric polarization nonlinear in the driving electric field. A quadratic response multiplies field components, creating sums and differences of their frequencies; second-harmonic generation is the equal-frequency sum case. Conversion strength also depends on phase matching and the material response.

Optical soliton

Words: 196 Articles: 4
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
An optical wave envelope whose spreading is balanced by nonlinear refraction. A temporal optical soliton balances dispersion, while a spatial optical soliton balances diffraction. Persistence of a profile in an ideal propagation model does not by itself establish robustness in a lossy, higher-dimensional or delayed-response medium.

Optical soliton OurBigBook.com
A localized temporal wave envelope supported by a balance of group velocity dispersion and self-phase modulation. Bright solitons decay to zero background; dark solitons are dips on a nonzero background. This temporal balance differs from the diffraction balance of a spatial optical soliton.

A dimensionless comparison of dispersion and self-phase modulation scales. For the focusing cubic fibre equation with a sech input, Ns​=1 gives a fundamental temporal bright soliton, and integer Ns​>1 gives an ideal higher-order temporal soliton. It is a scale parameter for an arbitrary initial pulse, not a theorem that the pulse contains exactly that many separated solitons.

Temporal optical soliton OurBigBook.com
An integer-order sech initial pulse in the ideal focusing cubic fibre equation has periodic shape evolution involving compression and recombination. It does not preserve a single fixed profile like a fundamental temporal bright soliton. Arbitrary noninteger-order initial pulses can contain radiation as well as solitons.

Dispersion and nonlinear lengths coincide. Higher-order corrections, attenuation and a delayed response can change actual propagation.

Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
Treat the strong input pump amplitudes as prescribed while solving for weaker fields. It is self-consistent only when conversion removes a small fraction of pump energy and the assumed pump phases remain valid. An apparent divergent gain is evidence of breakdown of this approximation, not unlimited energy generation.

Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
A third-order nonlinear optical susceptibility produces a polarization term proportional to E1​E2​E3∗​. Its temporal and spatial phases give the displayed output frequency and the source wave vector k1​+k2​−k3​. Efficient emission also requires that this source match a propagating optical mode. The pump waves supply the generated energy.

Four-wave mixing OurBigBook.com
All four interacting waves have the same frequency. Counterpropagating equal-frequency pumps can give a source proportional to the conjugate signal field, providing phase conjugation. The pump product must have the appropriate uniform spatial phase, and finite apertures and phase mismatch limit reconstruction.

Degenerate four-wave mixing OurBigBook.com
Because one wave travels backward, its incident boundary condition belongs at the opposite end of the medium. With u(0)=a and v(L)=0, differentiating once gives u′′=−κ2u and the solution
u(z)=acosκLcos[κ(L−z)]​,v(z)=ia∗cosκLsin[κ(L−z)]​.
(56)
The invariant ∣u∣2+∣v∣2 is constant along z, while the input/output powers obey transmission minus reflection equal to the incident power in this normalization. A proposed solution must satisfy both first-order equations, not just their second derivatives.

Backward four-wave-mixing boundary problem OurBigBook.com
The first zero of cosκL makes the homogeneous opposite-end boundary problem singular. Its undepleted-pump treatment admits a nontrivial field without an imposed signal, indicating a parametric oscillation threshold. Depletion, saturation and the actual noise-seeded dynamics determine finite fields near threshold.

For opposite equal pump wave vectors, a conjugate mixing source has wave vector −k3​. In an isotropic nondispersive medium this exactly matches a free backward wave at the generated frequency only in the degenerate case. Away from degeneracy the longitudinal mismatch has magnitude 2n∣ωP​−ω3​∣/c; a finite interaction length supplies a tolerance, not exact vector matching.

A beam with a transverse profile sustained by a balance between diffraction and a nonlinear change of refractive index. Existence in that model does not establish stability in two transverse dimensions or in a saturating, absorbing material.

Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
Loss of spatial overlap between interacting finite beams because their energy flux directions differ. In an anisotropic crystal, the direction of the Poynting vector need not coincide with the wave vector. For beam radius w and relative walk-off angle ρ, an overlap length is of order w/∣tanρ∣. A full conversion calculation also includes beam profiles, diffraction and phase mismatch.

Three-wave mixing

Words: 186 Articles: 5
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
An interaction among three waves mediated by a second-order nonlinear optical susceptibility. In sum-frequency generation, two input angular frequencies satisfy ω3​=ω1​+ω2​. The same coupling permits reverse conversion. Phase matching determines whether successive generated contributions reinforce; the Manley-Rowe relations express the associated lossless exchange constraints.

Manley-Rowe relations (I1′​/ω1​=I2′​/ω2​=−I3′​/ω3​)

Words: 88
Three-wave mixing OurBigBook.com
Conservation relations for resonant, lossless wave mixing. For sum-frequency generation with ω3​=ω1​+ω2​, the intensities obey I1′​/ω1​=I2′​/ω2​=−I3′​/ω3​. Thus I1​/ω1​+I3​/ω3​ and I2​/ω2​+I3​/ω3​ are constant. Their difference gives a third, dependent invariant. Adding the intensity derivatives yields conservation of energy.
The exchange interpretation divides each intensity by its photon energy ℏωj​. One conversion removes a photon from each lower-frequency mode and adds one to the upper mode. For classical coupled-wave equations, differentiating the squared complex amplitudes gives the same common exchange rate multiplied by (ω1​,ω2​,−ω3​). Loss or externally replenished pumps require corresponding source terms.

A nonlinear optics process producing a field at the sum of two input angular frequencies. The driven electric polarization contains a term proportional to the product of the input complex amplitudes. A nonzero initial output field also interferes with this generated field.

Kerr effect

Words: 320 Articles: 6
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
The Kerr effect is a change in a material's refractive index quadratic in an applied electric field. A static applied electric field can produce linear birefringence; the optical field itself can also produce an intensity-dependent refractive index in nonlinear optics.

Optical Kerr effect (n=n0​+n2​I)

Words: 243 Articles: 4
Kerr effect OurBigBook.com
An intensity-dependent refractive index produced by the optical field itself. In a simple instantaneous isotropic model, n=n0​+n2​I. A transversely nonuniform intensity produces self-focusing for positive n2​ and self-defocusing for negative n2​. Temporal intensity variation produces self-phase modulation. These are consequences of a third-order nonlinear optical susceptibility, distinct from a static applied-field electro-optic Kerr effect.
Cross-Kerr interaction (Hint​=ℏχn1​n2​)
Words: 152 Articles: 2
Optical Kerr effect OurBigBook.com
An ideal two-mode intensity-intensity coupling makes the phase of each mode depend on the other's photon number. With this sign convention, evolution for time t sends a mode-1 coherent amplitude to αe−iχtn2​ when mode 2 has definite occupation. This single-mode unitary model does not by itself establish a strong, noiseless interaction between real travelling single photons.

A one-photon polarization qubit can conditionally rotate another mode's coherent amplitude: the horizontal branch leaves α unchanged and the vertical branch gives αeiΘ. The output is generally entangled. Measuring the polarization in a superposition basis can erase the branch label and prepare a coherent superposition of the two amplitudes.

Polarization-controlled Kerr rotation OurBigBook.com
Normalize the initial polarization qubit and its analysing wave-plate transformation. At α=0,ϕ=π, that outcome has zero probability, explaining the singular normalization of the absent branch.

Optical Kerr effect OurBigBook.com
A beam's transverse intensity changes its own refractive index. For positive nonlinear index and a bright centre, the accumulated phase has the curvature of a converging lens. For I(r)=I0​e−2r2/w2 over a short length L, the in-medium thin-lens approximation gives 1/f=4n2​I0​L/(n0​w2). Negative n2​ instead produces self-defocusing.

Words: 48
Kerr effect OurBigBook.com
The electro-optic Kerr effect produces linear birefringence proportional to the square of a static applied electric field. Defining the Kerr effect coefficient K by Δn=λ0​KE2, a length L produces phase retardation δ=2πKLE2. A switchable quarter-wave plate requires ∣δ∣=π/2 modulo 2π, with fixed principal axes. This differs from the Faraday effect, whose eigenpolarizations are circular polarizations.

In spontaneous parametric down-conversion, a pump field drives a nonlinear optics process producing correlated pairs of photons.

Heralded single-photon source

Spontaneous parametric down-conversion OurBigBook.com
Detection of one member of a pair conditions the other mode towards a one-photon state. Imperfect collection reduces heralding efficiency; unresolved spectral correlations can leave a mixed state, and multiple pairs can contaminate the heralded output. Filtering can improve purity while reducing brightness. Heralding is conditional preparation, not deterministic conversion of every pump pulse.

The weak-gain state generated by an undepleted pump contains a vacuum term and a photon-pair amplitude. A continuum pair amplitude combines the pump spectrum with a phase-matching factor Lsinc(ΔkL/2)eiΔkL/2. Its joint spectrum determines spectral correlations and the purity attainable by heralding one partner.

SPDC pair state OurBigBook.com
For two collected spatial modes a,b, each with polarizations H,V, put K†=aH†​bV†​+aV†​bH†​. The one-pair state is a Bell state. The normalized two-pair component is
∣Ψ2​⟩=3​∣2Ha​,2Vb​⟩+∣Ha​Va​,Hb​Vb​⟩+∣2Va​,2Hb​⟩​.
(57)
This follows by expanding (K†)2 and using the bosonic creation operator identity (a†)n∣0⟩=n!​∣n⟩. The three orthogonal normalized Fock states have equal probability 1/3. A tensor product of independently labelled pairs is a different multimode description; identifying its labels without renormalization changes its norm.

For an ideal undepleted pump and one collected pair of spatial modes, the two orthogonal polarization-pair creation terms generate two commuting two-mode squeezed vacua. If λ=tanh2r, either squeezed pair has geometric occupation probability (1−λ)λk. Adding their pair counts gives n+1 equal-weight possibilities, hence Pn​=(n+1)(1−λ)2λn. Thus P1​=2(1−λ)2λ and P2​=3(1−λ)2λ2≃3P12​/4 at weak gain. Different unresolved temporal or spectral modes need not obey this single-mode formula.

Nonlinear optical susceptibility (χ(2))

Words: 571 Articles: 6
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
Choose one driving electric field component and one responding electric polarization component. A schematic local, instantaneous expansion is
P=ϵ0​(χ(1)E+χ(2)E2+χ(3)E3+⋯).
(58)
Here ϵ0​ is the vacuum permittivity, χ(1) is the linear electric susceptibility, and the higher coefficients describe nonlinear response. In SI, P has units Cm−2, E has units Vm−1, and χ(2) has units mV−1. The selected scalar coefficient depends on polarization of waves and crystal orientation; it is not a universal material number independent of geometry.
For a chosen monochromatic wave E(t)=E0​cosωt, the quadratic contribution is exactly
P(2)(t)=2ϵ0​χ(2)E02​​(1+cos2ωt).
(59)
The cosine identity separates a constant contribution, associated with optical rectification, from an oscillation at twice the angular frequency, the source for second-harmonic generation. A term oscillating at 2ω is a local driving source; efficient outgoing light additionally requires propagation and phase matching.
For a material with optical dispersion, the scalar instantaneous expansion is only a teaching model. The actual quadratic response is a tensor with output and input frequency arguments: χijk(2)​(2ω;ω,ω) describes the harmonic, whereas χijk(2)​(0;ω,−ω) describes the constant response. Their coefficients need not coincide. The cosine calculation establishes which frequencies are available, without assigning measured coefficients to any crystal.

Nonlinear-susceptibility tensor symmetry

Words: 258 Articles: 4
Nonlinear optical susceptibility OurBigBook.com
The order-n response has one output vector index and n input vector indices. Material point-group invariance, permutation of input index-frequency pairs, and reality of the electric polarization impose different constraints. They must not be conflated with the stronger dispersion-neglecting Kleinman symmetry.
Contracted nonlinear susceptibility notation (jk↦J∈{xx,yy,zz,yz,zx,xy})
Words: 67
Nonlinear-susceptibility tensor symmetry OurBigBook.com
For identical input frequencies, intrinsic permutation symmetry of nonlinear susceptibility makes the last two Cartesian indices symmetric. Store their six independent pairs as one index, so the quadratic response uses a three-by-six array diJ​. In the convention dijk​=χijk(2)​/2, the contracted input vector is (Ax2​,Ay2​,Az2​,2Ay​Az​,2Az​Ax​,2Ax​Ay​)T. The factors of two preserve the sum over both off-diagonal orderings. This bookkeeping does not assert the stronger Kleinman symmetry and does not change the tensor's physical order.
Isotropic fourth-rank susceptibility (χijkl​=aδij​δkl​+bδik​δjl​+cδil​δjk​)
Words: 49
Nonlinear-susceptibility tensor symmetry OurBigBook.com
An isotropic fourth-rank polar tensor has the displayed form. If its three input slots are fully interchangeable at the same relevant frequency arguments, then a=b=c, giving χxxxx​=3χxxyy​. For mixed-sign or unequal frequencies, intrinsic permutation exchanges the arguments too; it need not make all coefficients at one fixed ordering equal.
Kleinman symmetry
Words: 60
Nonlinear-susceptibility tensor symmetry OurBigBook.com
Far from relevant resonances, when frequency dispersion of the nonlinear response can be neglected, a susceptibility can acquire full permutation symmetry among spatial indices. For second order this reduces a general symmetric-input tensor's 18 components to 10 before material point-group reductions. Mere transparency does not establish this approximation. The name refers to D. A. Kleinman.[ref]
Intrinsic permutation symmetry of nonlinear susceptibility
Words: 43
Nonlinear-susceptibility tensor symmetry OurBigBook.com
Commuting input field factors permit the response kernel to be symmetrized under interchange of input index-frequency pairs. For example χijk(2)​(ωs​;ω1​,ω2​)=χikj(2)​(ωs​;ω2​,ω1​). This does not authorize exchanging indices while keeping unequal frequency arguments in their old slots, nor exchanging the output index without further assumptions.

Bulk electric-dipole selection rule (χ(2)=0)

Words: 142
Nonlinear optical susceptibility OurBigBook.com
Suppose a homogeneous bulk material is unchanged when all spatial coordinates are reversed. Both electric polarization and electric field reverse under this inversion, so a local electric dipole response must obey P(−E)=−P(E). Substituting the nonlinear optical susceptibility expansion gives
P(−E)+P(E)=2ϵ0​(χ(2)E2+χ(4)E4+⋯)=0.
(60)
For every sufficiently small E, all even coefficients vanish. In the full tensor relation, two reversed input electric fields leave their product unchanged while the output electric polarization changes sign, forcing every bulk electric-dipole component of χ(2) to vanish.
The qualification matters: the argument assumes inversion symmetry, a local bulk electric dipole response, and no applied bias that breaks that symmetry. A surface breaks bulk inversion symmetry; spatially varying or magnetic responses also lie outside this local electric-dipole model. Thus detecting second-harmonic generation at a surface or through a weaker magnetic contribution does not contradict the bulk selection rule. Conversely, absence of inversion symmetry permits some quadratic components but does not guarantee a nonzero component in every beam geometry.

Optical rectification

Words: 52
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
A static or slowly varying electric polarization produced by nonlinear response to an oscillating optical electric field. The constant term in nonlinear optical susceptibility is its simplest model. An optical pulse has a varying envelope, so its cycle-averaged quadratic response can vary during the pulse rather than remaining constant forever. This term alone does not imply a radiated zero-frequency wave.

Second-harmonic generation

Words: 850 Articles: 5
Nonlinear optics OurBigBook.com
Second-harmonic generation converts an incident optical frequency ν into 2ν through a material's nonlinear response. In the photon description of an ideal lossless conversion, two input photons supply one output photon:
2hν=h(2ν),ω=2πν.
(61)
Here h is the Planck constant. The relation states conservation of energy; the material mediates the interaction. It does not say that each input photon independently splits its wavelength in half.
For vacuum wavelengths, λ0,ω​=c/ν and λ0,2ω​=c/(2ν), where c is the speed of light. Hence
λ0,2ω​=2λ0,ω​​,λmed,ω​λmed,2ω​​=2n2ω​nω​​.
(62)
The second relation uses the refractive index for each propagating mode and frequency. Within a medium with optical dispersion, the wavelength need not halve. For an invented example, λ0,ω​=800nm, nω​=1.5, and n2ω​=1.6 give 400nm in vacuum, but in the material the two wavelengths are 533.33nm and 250nm; their ratio is 0.46875.

Two-crystal second-harmonic interference (I2ω​=4α2I02​L2cos2(Δkg​d/2))

Words: 62
Second-harmonic generation OurBigBook.com
Two identical phase-matched crystals generate coherent harmonic amplitudes. In a dispersive gap, the harmonic from the first crystal accumulates a different phase from twice the transmitted pump phase. Their interference gives the displayed undepleted-pump intensity in the stated equal-coupling amplitude normalization. Depletion changes the fringe shape; in the ideal lossless identical-crystal model, an opposite relative phase can coherently undo the first conversion.

Franken and colleagues frequency-doubling experiment

Words: 178
Second-harmonic generation OurBigBook.com
In 1961, Peter Alden Franken, Alan Hill, C. Wilbur Peters and Gabriel Weinreich focused a pulsed ruby laser through a red optical filter into quartz. The filter suppressed xenon-flash background. A quartz-prism spectrograph used red-insensitive Eastman Type 103 plates. A single shot recorded a feature near 347.2nm from 694.3nm input. Removing the quartz or substituting glass removed the feature; changing polarization of waves and orientation followed their predicted pattern. These controls supported second-harmonic generation; photographic density gave an estimated yield.[ref]
A spectrograph turns output frequency into a recording position. Its spectral separation makes a faint new component distinguishable from bright input light. The reported rounded wavelengths do not constitute an independent precision measurement of the ratio two. Nor do these observations demonstrate perfect phase matching or complete conversion. The experiment and Nicolaas Bloembergen's later theoretical account are distinct contributions to nonlinear optics.

Phase matching in second-harmonic generation (Δk=0)

Words: 492 Articles: 2
Second-harmonic generation OurBigBook.com
Phase matching makes wave amplitudes emitted at different depths add coherently. Consider collinear plane waves in a uniform transparent material of length L, with fixed polarization of waves and nonzero selected nonlinear optical susceptibility. Assume negligible pump depletion, negligible absorption, an initially absent harmonic, and a wide beam for which diffraction is negligible. The pump's wave amplitude is then constant throughout the interaction.
The pump electric field has spatial wave phase kω​z; its quadratic source has spatial wave phase 2kω​z. The freely propagating harmonic has wave number k2ω​. Define the second-harmonic phase mismatch by
Δk=k2ω​−2kω​,kω​=cnω​ω​,k2ω​=c2n2ω​ω​.
(63)
For the chosen complex-field convention, the outgoing harmonic wave amplitude, up to an overall constant and propagation phase, is proportional to
A(L)=∫0L​eiΔkzdz=LeiΔkL/2sinc(2ΔkL​),sincx={sinx/x,1,​x=0,x=0.​
(64)
Choosing the conjugate complex-field convention reverses the exponent's sign without changing the wave intensity. Taking the squared complex modulus gives
I2ω​(L)=CIω2​L2sinc2(2ΔkL​),C>0.
(65)
Here C is fixed for the chosen modes and material; its dimensions accommodate the stated wave intensity convention. The quadratic pump dependence follows because the source wave amplitude is proportional to E02​, whereas Iω​ is proportional to E02​. The sinc function comes from summing contributions along the whole material, just as a finite aperture produces diffraction through addition of complex amplitudes.
At Δk=0, the integral is L and the harmonic wave intensity grows as L2. At ΔkL=2π, all those contributions cancel. This cancellation needs no absorption: their wave phases wind through a full turn. At high conversion, the constant-pump assumption fails, so the L2 law cannot continue indefinitely. Tight focusing, finite optical pulses, absorption, and transverse separation of modes also require a more complete model.
Optical dispersion generally makes n2ω​=nω​. In a suitable crystal, birefringence allows modes with different polarization of waves to experience different refractive indices, making their selected values equal. The appropriate crystal direction and allowed nonlinear optical susceptibility component must both work.[ref]
For a worked calculation, choose L0​=1mm and Δk=πmm−1. At L=L0​, the harmonic wave intensity is 4/π2≃0.4053 of its perfectly matched value. At L=2L0​ it vanishes in this model. More material can therefore reduce the output. If instead Δk=0, doubling L multiplies output by four. The two curves retain that common normalization, so their different peak heights are meaningful.
Second-harmonic phase mismatch (Δk=k2ω​−2kω​)
Words: 33
Phase matching in second-harmonic generation OurBigBook.com
The difference between the harmonic's wave number and that of the quadratic driving electric polarization. It has units of inverse length. For collinear modes, Δk=2ω(n2ω​−nω​)/c, so matching frequencies alone does not ensure matching spatial wave phases.
Second-harmonic coherence length (Lc​=π/∣Δk∣)
Words: 52
Phase matching in second-harmonic generation OurBigBook.com
The length over which the harmonic and its quadratic source accumulate a relative wave phase of π. For nonzero second-harmonic phase mismatch, Lc​=π/∣Δk∣; the first output zero of the uniform undepleted model occurs at 2Lc​. This is a propagation mismatch length, distinct from the pump's optical coherence length. It diverges as perfect phase matching is approached.
